Huang was said to be "contrite" about his behavior, and the board was satisfied after it explained the importance of "candor and honesty" in the future.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Following the news that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang has returned to the company as CEO a little more than a week after he resigned from the role, it's now believed that he admitted to additional extra-marital affairs beyond the two that were already known. The admission came during an hours-long meeting with Huang as Nvidia's board members discussed him potentially coming back to a company he left in disarray when he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, worked for Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer that is now under criminal investigation over its possible involvement in the smuggling of export-controlled Nvidia AI chips into China. Now, with Huang back in the top job at Nvidia, a WSJ report claims that the company's board rehired him despite the revelation that his affairs outnumbered the two already reported.

The report details a November 22 meeting in which Huang and the Nvidia board sat down to discuss his return. Huang told the board that there were more affairs than those it already knew about, with people with knowledge of the discussions saying that he was contrite about his behavior. Then, after the board explained to Huang that it was important that he be honest and candid after at least one affair with an Nvidia employee, it was agreed that the best thing for the company would be for Huang to return. Huang has confessed to being unfaithful to his wife, Lori, reportedly carrying on an affair with Megaspeed's Alice Huang and Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell. The report explicitly states Huang admitted to multiple further affairs, bringing the total of known instances to at least four.

The company said its board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang. It's unclear whether its decision was affected by Nvidia's 24% stock price fall following Huang's affair scandal first broke. President Trump also stated he heavily lobbied for Huang's return, personally dialling in to an Nvidia board meeting to persuade the company to reinstate him.

“I’m terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this,” Huang reportedly said in a video of his return to the Nvidia offices. “I’ve made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.”

Huang's return to Nvidia came after a week of uncertainty for the company. Calls for his return were made by everyone from SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to U.S. President Trump. The latter was very vocal in his stance on Huang and has since taken the credit for Nvidia's decision to reinstate him. This came after he initially called for former Apple CEO Tim Cook to take the reins of the company.

One of Huang's first acts as the returning Nvidia CEO will be to appear before a House Foreign Affairs panel. He'll do so on December 1 to answer questions about his affair with Alice Huang in the context of import-controlled AI chips finding their way into China.

#10287. Which Samsung folding phone is right for you? Galaxy Z Fold 8, Ultra, or Flip 8

Folding phones are entering a new chapter and, if you’re looking to try one for the first time, you might not know exactly where to start. In this guide, we’ll take a look at some of the most important questions to answer when buying a foldable, and dissect how Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Galaxy Z Flip 8 fit the bill to figure out which is the best for you, especially if you’re interested in one this holiday season.

Samsung has three foldables in its lineup this year, two of which are pretty familiar. The Galaxy Z Flip 8 continues the lineup of clamshell-style foldables, offering a form factor similar to that of a classic flip phone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, meanwhile, is designed to be a normal smartphone on the outside, hiding a tablet within. Finally, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the new kid on the block, offering a compact outer display that opens up to a media-friendly, wider inner panel.

Each one serves a different need, but they all share similar performance and core specs. Here’s a quick rundown of the key details on each device:

Starting with the displays, the book-style Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra both provide outer displays that are fully usable as standard smartphones, while the inner display is useful for multitasking, media, or just getting more space for reading a website or e-book. Samsung’s top-tier specs deliver performance for everything you’d need, with Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy powering everything from demanding games or media-editing apps to day-to-day use.

With each Samsung foldable, you’re getting a fully capable smartphone, but finding the one that’s best for you is a matter of picking your most important priorities. Cameras, battery life, content consumption, and size are some of the most important points to consider, so let’s take a look one-by-one.

When it comes to cameras, foldables have a tough time. There’s only so much physical space to fit the camera sensors and, with cameras, having more space generally results in a battery overall camera.

That said, the best camera on a Samsung foldable is undoubtedly on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra has a 200MP main camera that’s similar to the Galaxy S26 Ultra, while it also packs a 50MP ultrawide and something neither of the others offer, a telephoto lens. The 10MP telephoto shooter captures faraway subjects at 3x optical zoom, meaning you’re not giving up on quality when you zoom in. Two 10MP cameras can be found on the displays, with neither sacrificing quality for an under-display look.

Runner-up here is the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which offers a pair of 50MP cameras for wide and ultrawide shots. You can get 2x optical-quality zoom out of the main sensor to still get a good zoom shot, while the main camera still offers good quality and Samsung’s best camera features including 2x optical-quality zoom and the subject-tracking My FanCam.

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 may not have the best camera hardware, but what it lacks in hardware it makes up for in flexibility. This is definitely the best form factor of the bunch for using the foldable design as a tripod for capturing clips. All three devices also use their foldable nature to let you capture full-quality selfies using the rear cameras, which always have better quality than the 10MP dedicated front-facing cameras.

Here’s where specs on paper can tell a different story compared to real life.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra may offer the biggest battery of the bunch at 5,000 mAh, but its battery life is on par with the smaller Galaxy Z Fold 8. Both foldables are designed to last you through a full day, though sticking to the outer display only on the Fold 8 Ultra may bring you slightly better battery life overall.

In either case, you’re also getting 45W fast charging over USB-C, granting you speedy recharging if your device happens to get low through the course of a busy day. These are also “Qi2 Ready,” meaning you can use magnetic wireless chargers if you use a compatible magnetic case.

One of the most important things you’ll want to ask yourself when buying a foldable phone is why you want to opt for a foldable in the first place, and each of these devices gives a different answer.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is a productivity powerhouse, delivering more space on its inner display for you to get work done through the web, apps, and more. You can run up to three apps at once on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s display, as well as floating apps, and more.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 is great for media consumption. The wider aspect ratio is perfect for watching videos, playing games, reading books, and more, all while still giving you plenty of space for productivity just like the Ultra.

Galaxy Z Flip 8, meanwhile, is all about giving you a more compact device. The outer display lets you quickly reply to messages or keep up with directions, while you can unfold it to do everything you want to on a normal phone. Close it up to more easily stow it away in your pocket or your bag.

If you are moving into a new Galaxy foldable, the good news is that you don’t have to start from scratch. Thanks to Samsung’s Smart Switch app, you can easily transfer supported content including pictures, contacts, messages, and more from an older Galaxy phone, another Android phone, or even an iPhone over to a Galaxy foldable. Apps, messages, photos, and more can all make the move wirelessly, without the need of a cable.

You can get the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra, and Flip 8 from your favorite carriers and retailers, but Best Buy is one of the best places to score a great deal with solid trade-in values and deep discounts around Black Friday and throughout the holiday season.

#10286. AI upended entry-level jobs. Here’s what employers are actually looking for

AI is changing nearly every aspect of the workplace—but especially entry-level jobs, to the point where Gen Z is calling for millennials (who are only in their 30s and 40s) to retire to make room. Many are placing the blame on AI for making tasks in many entry-level jobs outdated; data seems to back that up.

A recent survey of nearly 7,000 workers, managers, and executives found that 51% believe AI is reducing early-career opportunities, while 49% say tasks that traditionally helped employees build work experience are increasingly being handled by AI. Another shows that entry-level listings have plummeted 35% since 2023; another suggests entry-level jobs in New York City have been cut in half.

That means the pressure is on for early-career candidates to show employers what they can bring to a role beyond their ability to use AI tools. A catch-22 emerges: many employers increasingly turn to AI, yet many also want candidates who can think independently, come up with original ideas, recognize when to put the technology aside and trust their own judgment.

Indeed, many young workers find themselves in a tricky-to-navigate, even unfair entry-level job market. Luckily, there are tips that can make you stand out in a labor market that both increasingly relies on AI, and that also demands workers show employers the human skills they’re looking for.

Don’t let AI write your resume for you

Sure, AI can be a helpful writing tool: it can help you brainstorm, organize your experience, even give you a first draft. But if every candidate is using AI to write their application, it can become harder to show what makes you different. According to Amitoj Sandhu, Manager of Global Early Talent at HR platform Dayforce, employers are starting to see more applications that all sound alike.

“Every single profile looks the same. They all are the same on the paper, so it becomes really hard for us to shortlist them and present in front of leaders,” he says.

Sandhu says AI is a useful starting point, but candidates need to be able to use their own voice, and  stand behind what they submit. After all, if AI is writing your resume for you, when it comes time for the interview, “will you be able to validate the results?” he says.

Sandhu recommends preparing two or three strong examples from internships, school projects, or extracurricular activities that you can actually speak to authentically without farming everything out to ChatGPT. Then, be ready to walk an interviewer through those experiences and what you learned from them.

With fewer entry-level roles apparently available, layering this in can make your application pop.

Do use AI in your cover letter, but with caution

“AI can be a great tool for writing a better cover letter. It can help candidates organize their ideas, communicate more clearly and make meaningful connections between their own interests and the company they’re applying to,” says Dan Kejsefman, Talent Director at Avature, a software development company. 

He says AI can raise the bar in terms of an application’s quality—but at the same time, “the motivation behind it still needs to be genuine.” 

“I’d encourage candidates to start with their own reasons for wanting the job: What interests them about the company? What would they like to learn? What experiences or interests connect them to the opportunity? Then use AI to help communicate those ideas more effectively,” he says.

The important thing is being able to explain and stand behind what’s in your cover letter. 

“AI can help you tell your story better,” he says, “but the story still has to be yours.” Use AI tools where you can—many jobs will expect you to use them to some extent, anyway—but standing out in an increasingly crowded entry-level field means tapping into what makes you, you.

Don’t leave your curiosity at home

According to Sandhu, when it comes time for the interview, curiosity is one of the biggest qualities employers look for. Missing that in an interview is “kind of a red flag for us,” Sandhu says.

Sure, one way to demonstrate this is by researching the employer before the interview, and developing a genuine understanding of what the company does and the industry it operates in. But preparation is only part of it. 

Kejsefman says candidates also need to show genuine interest in the conversation, rather than simply relying on a list of questions prepared with AI during your interview practice.

“AI can help candidates research a company, understand a role, and prepare thoughtful questions. That’s useful, and I wouldn’t discourage it,” Kejsefman explains. “But there’s a difference between asking an impressive question, and actually being interested in understanding the answer.”

For example, curious candidates listen carefully, ask follow-up questions and try to understand why things work the way they do. That’s a timeless strategy, regardless of AI or not.

Young workers “don’t necessarily have all the answers, and that’s perfectly fine, especially early in their careers. What matters is whether they show a real desire to learn and understand,” Kejsefman says.

Do bring your own judgment to the work

Sandhu says employers want candidates who can question the information AI provides, apply their own judgment and build on what the technology produces.

Think of a software developer who might use ChatGPT to generate code, but still needs to determine whether it makes sense or meets the requirements or passes the right tests. Human judgment, after all, has long been touted as something that will still prove crucial in the AI era—in fact, as more decisions get outsourced to robots, it becomes even more valuable.

“Can you use your own judgment to evaluate a response you get from AI? Can you build on that context? That’s what we’re looking for,” Sandhu says.

In fields such as communications and journalism, employers still want to see creativity and original ideas rather than generic content generated by AI. “They want to look at how you think and what kind of ideas you can spark, not just all the generic ideas AI is producing,” Sandhu says.

Kejsefman says AI adoption is still uneven across organizations, creating an opportunity for early-career professionals. A recent graduate who develops strong AI skills can bring something valuable to a team, even when working alongside people with much more professional experience. But they also bring enthusiasm and perspective older workers don’t have, and that robots definitely don’t have.

Kejsefman also cautions against focusing exclusively on learning individual AI tools. As those tools continue to change, the ability to think critically, understand problems and evaluate results will become increasingly important. 

As AI takes on more workplace tasks, your ability to bring your own ideas, judgment and perspective to the work can help you stand out—especially when looking to break into a field or organization.

Do prioritize experience over job titles

Regardless of best practices, as AI continues to change the skills employers need, recent graduates may need to be more flexible about where they start their careers. For starters, Sandhu cautions against focusing too heavily on a particular job title or starting salary.

“The big mistake which they’re making is they’re running after titles and what the compensation is going to look like,” Sandhu says.

Instead, he encouraged candidates to prioritize gaining experience and finding opportunities to get started, even if the position isn’t exactly what they initially envisioned or in their precisely preferred field.

“Don’t run after a specific job title in the world which is changing every day,” he says.

And that experience doesn’t have to come from a traditional job. Kejsefman encourages recent graduates to draw on those other past experiences, like university projects or volunteering—even personal projects or side gigs, which a lot of Gen Z already has anyway.

“They need examples of situations where they’ve taken initiative, faced a problem, learned something new, or adapted when things didn’t go as expected,” Kejsefman says. 

“For someone starting their career, demonstrating that mindset can be much more valuable than presenting a perfectly polished result.”

Make no mistake—for new workers in the workplace, it’s rough out there. But keeping these strategies, which mix time-tested tactics with AI adoption and adaptation, could open the right door at the right time.

Project Leonida is no more, even after the project got GTA 6 to run on a PC, with the person behind it now banned from Discord for two years.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Project Leonida, a recompilation project aiming to bring the console version of GTA 6 to the PC, has been shut down, with its Discord and GitHub servers taken offline. The 15-year-old kid behind the project has admitted that Rockstar took down the server, adding that the life of a teenager is hard enough "without having middle-aged men yell and complain to you on Discord." The Project Leonida Discord server had almost 180,000 members when it was taken offline, TechPowerUp reports. NotRezed, the account behind the project and associated online presences, has also confirmed that they have been banned from Discord for two years.

The project to make GTA 6 run on a Windows PC months ahead of the game's expected early 2027 release window is one of a run of similar recompilations, some of which have proven successful. Earlier this year, we saw Zelda: Ocarina of Time brought to Apple platforms, months before the game's remake was announced for the Nintendo Switch 2. That same game is now circulating online after an AI-assisted jailbreak allowed it to be dumped immediately following its release. Similar AI assistance has helped the recompilation efforts of multiple projects in recent months, and GTA 6 is unlikely to be the last.

In the case of this ill-fated project, it came just days after notorious leaker Cyberleek made a near-complete build of the Xbox version of GTA 6 available online. A missing executable for the game was then also released on November 23, with recompilation efforts taking note. And while Project Leonida is no more, there's no indication that other parallel projects will follow suit.

As for NotRexed, they say that they "really want to make cool stuff," but that things have happened that they "can't control," and they will be stepping away as a result.

GTA 6 was released on the PS5 and Xbox Series X|S platforms on November 19 and immediately shot to the top of sales charts. It's since been confirmed that the game reached $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales with 32.5 million units sold pre-release. Sony has also announced that the game set a new record for the highest number of concurrent players on PlayStation, with players logging 683 million hours of gameplay by November 23. The game has captured the attention of gamers everywhere, with one even using mind control and eye tracking to hijack an in-game airplane.

#10284. Getting asked why you haven’t bought a house this Thanksgiving? Here’s what to tell your relatives

It’s bad enough you have to sleep on the pull-out couch for a few days, but then come the questions.

If the topic of homeownership—and, more pointedly, why you don’t yet own a home—comes up at Thanksgiving, here’s a stat to keep your pestering relatives at bay. A household today earning a median income would need to save for 10.5 years to have enough for a 10% down payment on a median-priced home—that’s more than three times longer than in the 1980s, according to a new report from Realtor.com.

While your relatives may bemoan the double-digit mortgage rates of the 1980s, homes on the market were relatively more affordable. That’s because the surge in home prices, and especially in recent years, has far outpaced the rise in wages, which is keeping many prospective homebuyers on the sidelines, according to the Austin-based real estate site.

“The reality is that today’s aspiring buyers face a different housing market than generations before,” Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in a statement. And it’s not just that home prices have outpaced wage growth, homebuyers are also facing rising costs for insurance and homeowners association (HOA) fees that are stretching their budgets, she added. “The path to homeownership has become increasingly difficult.”

In the 1980s, the median-priced home was selling for roughly 3.2 times the typical annual household income at the time, according to Realtor.com. Today, shoppers are trying to squeeze into a market where homes are selling for 4.8 times the typical household income. It’s no wonder, then, that so many younger people are living at home for longer to save up for a down payment when a first-time homebuyer is now 40 years old.

WHERE HOUSING IS MORE, LESS AFFORDABLE

Depending on where you live, you might already have an arsenal of mind-blowing stats about your local housing market. In some major metro areas, saving enough money for a down payment for a median-priced home has become a herculean task unto itself.

People earning the median income could understandably feel locked out of the housing market in many areas. Among the 50 largest metro areas, the five where workers must save the longest for a 10% down payment on a median-priced home are: 

  • Los Angeles, California: 24.8 years
  • San Diego, California: 18.8 years
  • San Jose, California: 18.4 years
  • New York, New York: 17.0 years
  • Boston, Massachusetts: 15.7 years

On the flip side, saving up for a down payment in the following five metro areas could happen in the span of less than a decade for some households:

  • Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania: 7.2 years
  • Detroit, Michigan: 7.6 years
  • St. Louis, Missouri: 7.6 years
  • Buffalo, New York: 7.9 years
  • Cleveland, Ohio: 8.1 years

Of course, housing-related costs aren’t limited to saving up for the down payment and then budgeting for monthly mortgage payments. Homeowners today must also factor in the rising costs of things like insurance or HOA fees at a time when the price of, well, everything seems to be going up.

“For many younger Americans, the challenge isn’t a lack of willingness to save,” Jones said. “It’s that the financial goalposts have moved.”

#10282. ‘Galaxy Watch 10’ won’t launch in 2027 as Samsung tries to slow RAMageddon losses

According to a new report, Samsung’s next “Galaxy Watch 10” won’t be releasing in 2027 with the company moving to a bi-yearly release schedule for its smartwatches.

ETNews reports that Samsung will not have a new Galaxy Watch model releasing in 2027, a series that would have likely been called “Galaxy Watch 10.” The reason, the report suggests, is that Samsung is “undertaking a structural overhaul to strengthen profitability” (translated) following two quarters in a row of losses in its mobile division.

Samsung has released a new Galaxy Watch every year since 2018, with 2021’s Galaxy Watch 4 marking the switch to Wear OS.

The new schedule will apparently see new Galaxy Watch releases every other year, pushing the next release into 2028. The report goes on to mention that Galaxy Watch is part of a “mature phase” of the smartwatch market, and that Galaxy Watch 9 sales “fell short of expectations” likely due in part to its higher price point.

Apparently, Samsung plans new Galaxy Watch software updates next year as well as “enhancement of healthcare features.” The Galaxy Fit 4 fitness tracker is also expected in 2027, with Dealabs reporting that the tracker will be priced at €79.90 in Europe, a slight price hike over the previous release.

#10281. Dollar Tree’s stock is skyrocketing. One number in its earnings report helps explain why

The broader markets are seeing red today, primarily led lower by yet another steep selloff in technology and artificial intelligence stocks. But one company nearly as far from those sectors as you can get is seeing its share price surge by over 10% today: the discount retailer Dollar Tree. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

This morning, the discount retail chain Dollar Tree, Inc. (Nasdaq: DLTR) reported its third-quarter fiscal 2026 results, which cover the three-month period ending October 31. The most salient metrics from those results are as follows:

  • Net sales: $5.1 billion
  • Adjusted earnings per share (EPS): $1.16
  • Comparable store net sales: up 4.6%
  • Foot traffic increase: 3.8%
  • New stores: 84
  • Total stores: 9,511

To put those financials in perspective, LSEG analysts estimated $5.04 billion in net sales and earnings per share of 91 cents, notes Reuters. 

Announcing the company’s Q3 results, Dollar Tree CEO Mike Creedon said, “Our third quarter results show the strength of Dollar Tree’s value proposition and the progress we’ve made to improve the customer experience. Comp traffic accelerated to 3.8% and drove comparable sales above the high end of our outlook. Our broader assortment, better stores and stronger customer engagement give shoppers more reasons to choose Dollar Tree and come back more often.”

Why are Dollar Tree’s shares surging?

After announcing its Q3, DLTR stock surged—one of the few to do so today on Wall Street.

Dollar Tree’s price jump comes down to a few factors, both of which seem to have pleased investors, based on the company’s share price.

The first was the net sales and earnings per share beat. Net sales increased by 6.9% versus the same quarter a year earlier. This was helped by a 4.6% increase in comparable net store sales. Those comps were driven by a 3.8% increase in foot traffic and a 0.8% increase in the amount people spend on an average ticket.

In other words, most of the comp increase was not driven by higher tickets, but by increased foot traffic—which is exactly what you want as you enter the final quarter of the year: the all-important holiday period.

In addition to favorable quarterly results, another factor that buoyed investors’ view of the company was its full-year fiscal 2026 outlook. 

Dollar Tree increased its full-year earnings per share range to between $8.05 and $8.25. That was up from its prior range of $7.70 to $8.05.

DLTR’s up more than 60% in six months

As of the time of this writing, DLTR shares are currently trading up 11% to $154.41 on the back of its Q3 results. That’s an exceptional one-day jump for a discount retailer, but it goes to show the faith investors currently have in the company, which may be one of the few to benefit from an inflation-wary consumer.

As prices rise, people tend to cut back on discretionary spending, which can cause downward pressure on retailer shares. But as everyday costs get higher, consumers also tend to shop around for the best price for essentials and everyday items.

Dollar Tree has a low-cost pricing structure (many items cost around $1.25, with higher-priced items selling for between $3 and $7) that appeals to cash-strapped consumers operating in an economy where sticker prices at higher-end retailers seem increasingly out of reach.

While the company’s roughly 11% share price jump today (as of the time of this writing) is impressive, looking back a little further reveals even better stock price growth. In the past month alone, DLTR shares are up 22%, and over the past six months, DLTR shares are up 61%.

#10280. Find Orphan Pages and Buried Content: Build an Internal Link Graph for Your Site

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The pages of a site form a graph. Think of it as many nodes connected to each other via edges. Each of the edges are the links between the pages, and the nodes themselves are the pages. Now if you start to visualize this as a graph, you will quickly see that there are multiple ways to traverse this graph and reach a particular endpoint.

A search crawler usually uses one of these pages as a starting point and crawls through all of the pages (especially when pages are not fully covered in a sitemap).

If a page lies very deep from the home page, it means that it's not an important page. It's an indication to the search engine that this is not something that you yourself consider important, and the search engine has a lesser incentive to rank this page over pages that are linked better within your site.

The key metric here is link depth. That is the number of clicks it takes to reach a particular page from your home page.

Another key metric is broken links. If you have too many broken links, it indicates to the search engine that your site is outdated and not well maintained, and the search engine will then not want to rank your site.

The way to identify both these problems is the same: to actually walk through your site, do a crawl of your site outside in, and try to figure out what the link depth is and if there are broken links on your website.

Seed the crawl with the home page and all URLs mentioned in the sitemap. Technically, the sitemap is not required if you're doing a crawl, but going from the sitemap will allow us to detect orphaned pages as well.

Fetch the pages and follow redirects as required. Record when you're following a redirect: we do not let fetch follow it silently, we record each hop and add its target to the crawl. Record HTTP errors as they occur.

Drop URL fragments and tracking parameters. Keep trailing slashes because sometimes there can be mismatches around expectation of trailing slashes in different URLs of a site.

In order to navigate from the home page, we can use BFS. So we know that the first time we reach a page, that is the page's shortest path.

We can cut off the depth over a certain threshold, say 5, to indicate that pages beyond that are too far or too deep to be reached.

Noindex pages will still be crawled. However, we need to make a record of them being not indexed, to reflect that they will not be present in the search engine.

The desired page depth is as close to the home page as possible. Important pages should be close to the home page. The deeper you go from the home page, it signals to the search engine that the page is less important.

A couple of examples of how a deep page is present:

The suggested fix for this is that we link the pages from as close to the home page as possible:

Wasted links are those internal links that do not do the job they're supposed to do. The different types of wasted links:

We have seen here how to look at our own website through the lens of a search engine. You can use some of the code over here to create your own crawler and identify internal linking issues; the full script is in this gist. Alternatively, we can use a free internal link visualizer to identify these issues and focus only on the fixes to improve our site's internal linking.

#10277. 94% of the world’s biggest songs have one surprising thing in common

While there is still no recipe for becoming a globally recognized musician, there is one thing that is consistently getting artists on the charts: TikTok.

TikTok’s recent 2026 Music Impact Report found that 94% of songs that entered the Billboard top 200 chart this year went viral on TikTok first. The link is stronger than before: in 2024, TikTok found that 84% of songs on the charts had gone viral on the platform first,  up ten percentage points in two years.

TikTok virality also affects how long a song stays on the chart. The report also found that tracks that went viral on the platform stayed on the charts for four times longer than those that didn’t catch a moment of popularity on the platform. For instance, songs that had a viral moment on TikTok would spend eight weeks on Billboard charts, as opposed to just two weeks for non-viral hits.

But the charts are not the only metric artists use to measure their success and growth, their performance on streaming platforms matters too. The report also found that TikTok virality influences streaming, with 74% of the fastest-growing artists on streaming platforms saw their streams rise alongside their views on TikTok.

Sienna Spiro is among the breakthrough artists who rose to fame through the platform, starting her career singing songs to a small audience on TikTok, eventually landing on the VMA stage this year singing her hit song Great Expectations.

While a relatively small artist just a year ago, she found a viral moment in her song Die on This Hill, with millions of fans using the sound for their TikToks, giving her recognition beyond the platform. 

Additionally, the platform’s new “add to music app” feature, which lets users connect their TikTok to their streaming service to automatically save songs from videos to their playlists, contributed to Spiro’s streaming success. According to the report, millions of users used the feature to save the single to their music apps. Spiro’s viral hit led her to enter the top 20 of the Billboard Hot 100, where it stayed for 13 weeks.

#10275. Why your HSA needs a succession plan

Health savings accounts are usually discussed in the context of their trifecta of tax benefits: pretax money going in, tax-free compounding while the funds are inside the account, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified healthcare expenditures.

But HSAs have their limits. The HSA’s tax benefits effectively cease upon the account owner’s death, or the death of his or her spouse if that person is the beneficiary.

That makes it crucial to have a succession plan for your HSA: a plan to encourage tax-free spending during your lifetime (and your spouse’s, if you have one), as well as naming the correct beneficiary for the account to maximize the tax benefits.

HSAs give during your lifetime . . .

Whereas tax-sheltered retirement account owners will pay taxes on the dollars they put into a retirement account (Roth) or on their withdrawals (traditional tax-deferred), HSAs are a unicorn account type—the funds are tax-free every step of the way, provided you spend the money on qualified healthcare expenses.

Those tax benefits are magnified for people who pay their healthcare expenses out of pocket, invest in long-term investment assets, and are in higher tax brackets.

Given those prodigious tax benefits, an HSA investor would have a bigger balance than a person investing in an IRA, 401(k), or taxable brokerage account, assuming the same contribution amounts, rates of return, tax rates, and holding periods. That’s because investors in those other account types pay taxes along the way: at time of contribution (Roth), during accumulation (taxable), and/or at time of withdrawal (taxable, traditional tax-deferred).

. . . And take after death

If your spouse is the designated beneficiary of your HSA, the HSA becomes theirs after your death, and the tax benefits continue. They can continue to take tax-free withdrawals for qualified healthcare expenses.

But if a person other than your spouse inherits the HSA, the account becomes less attractive than the other key account types mentioned before. An HSA inherited by a nonspouse beneficiary effectively ceases to be an HSA upon the account owner’s death, and all of its tax benefits go away at that time. Moreover, the nonspouse beneficiary will need to include the inherited HSA amount in their income and pay taxes on it.

The tax treatment of an HSA inherited by a nonspouse beneficiary is a bit worse than the tax treatment of other major account types that nonspouse beneficiaries might inherit. Heirs enjoy tax-free withdrawals on inherited Roth accounts. Traditional IRA beneficiaries owe taxes, but they at least enjoy some flexibility on the timing of their withdrawals and tax bills. Heirs inheriting taxable accounts have it even better, in that their cost basis becomes whatever the account holdings’ values were on the date of your death.

You need a plan for handling your HSA

That meh tax treatment on HSAs inherited by nonspouse beneficiaries highlights the value of having a plan to maximize your HSA’s long-term tax benefits.

Step 1: Get a system for spending from it

Spending from the HSA during your and your spouse’s lifetimes is key, so every HSA owner needs a spending plan. That’s true whether you’re paying healthcare expenses as you incur them or investing the funds for retirement.

If you’ve been paying your healthcare costs out of pocket in an effort to allow your account to grow, you can later use the HSA for non-healthcare expenses, provided you have receipts to substantiate those previous out-of-pocket healthcare costs. Ideally, you’d scan and document those expenditures as you incur them. If you’re a married person who’s overseeing your household’s HSA, make sure your spouse understands the withdrawal rules, where to find receipts, and how to submit them to the HSA provider.

Step 2: Assign the correct beneficiaries

Next, give care to naming beneficiaries. If you’re married, your spouse is a sensible beneficiary for the HSA; as noted earlier, they will be able to take over ownership of the account after your death and keep its full tax benefits during their lifetime.

Nonspouse beneficiaries won’t receive the same favorable tax treatment. However, if you think a nonspouse beneficiary still will benefit from the money, that’s probably a good enough reason to leave them the HSA. But other accounts should take precedence.

A charity can also make an excellent HSA beneficiary, as the charity won’t need to pay taxes on that amount. That strategy can be particularly appropriate for single people who are charitably inclined, or for surviving spouses. If you’re married, consider making your spouse the primary beneficiary and a charity the secondary.

Step 3: Make sure your beneficiaries understand the rules about HSAs

If your spouse will inherit your HSA, be sure to underscore the value of liquidating the account during his or her lifetime.

While it’s generally not advisable for a nonspouse beneficiary to inherit an HSA, if that’s your plan, it’s important to let your loved ones know that they can reduce the taxable amount in the HSA by paying any of your unpaid medical bills from the HSA. They just need to pay those bills out of your HSA within a year of your death.

This article was provided to The Associated Press by Morningstar. For more retirement content, go to morningstar.com/retirement.

The latest in 3D printing tech comes to Frankfurt.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Once a year, all the world’s 3D printing manufacturers gather for Formnext in Frankfurt, Germany, to showcase new technologies, software, and ideas. This year’s show was more compact, with three halls instead of four, but consumer 3D printers had a larger presence. Spread across two halls, we found Bambu Lab, Prusa Research, Snapmaker, Creality, Elegoo, Anycubic, and Flashforge, plus a few newbies like Axiloop.

Startup SnowX was a popular booth, presenting the first consumer-grade desktop metal 3D printer coming soon to Kickstarter.

I counted ten tool-changing 3D printers on the show floor, five of which I’ve already reviewed. Elegoo surprised us all by launching its Centauri X Ultra four-color tool changer at the show, while Axiloop’s MC 8 arrived on my front porch that morning.

Only Anycubic is standing pat with a single-nozzle multicolor machine. Instead, it presented its new partnership with Thingiverse.

Full-color UV printers were on display as well, with Flashforge showing off its CJ270, which was teased last year.

Editor’s Note: Snapmaker provided travel accommodations for this trip. Coverage remains editorially independent.

Bambu Lab showed off its latest printers, the H3C, a tool changer (starting at $2,499) with nine lightweight tools we reviewed earlier in the month, and its first laser, the R1, reviewed in September, which retails at $2,499.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

More interesting is the launch of “Bambu Circle,” a pilot program that will start in the Netherlands and slowly expand across Europe. The goal is a network of local hubs to assist entrepreneurs with their 3D printing side hustle. Bambu Circle would enlist repair specialists and community ambassadors to provide a helping hand and an in-person retail shop with space for meetups. ,

At the moment, there is no plan to launch a similar program in the United States; however, we have many retailers here who offer official warranty support, parts, and tons of filament. A map on the Bambu Lab lists 31 US resellers, though that number is a bit skewed since there are also 31 MicroCenters in the US.

Prusa Research previewed the Rugged, a CORE One L+ adapted for printing in the harshest environments. The printer has a sealed case that keeps out both humidity and dust while providing extra protection during transport for machines used in the field. The CORE One L+ tucked inside is equipped with a high-temperature, hardened steel nozzle for printing advanced engineering filaments. It also comes with Prusa’s Zero-Trace system, which is an air-gapped machine with no flash drive storage, no USB slot, no Wi-Fi, and no camera. They can only accept files from your own cryptographically paired Prusa Connect server. These extremely secure, extremely tough machines are meant for classified and proprietary work environments.

However, you don’t need to have a security clearance to jump on board Prusa Connect Local, a free-to-use version of Prusa Connect for anyone who wishes to keep their 3D printers off the internet. The server can run on Linux, Windows, Mac, or a Raspberry Pi, and can handle a print farm of two to 400. It’s currently set up for any Prusa Printer, but it is open source, so you are free to tinker around with it and add your own extensions.

Snapmaker showed off what you can do with its four-color U1 tool changer. Ratdoux, the developer behind Full Spectrum, was on hand to chat with us. He devised a system of color-blending filaments that take thin layers of cyan, yellow, and magenta mixed with either gray or white, which can create nearly any other color. He said it was inspired by a conversation on Reddit where users were mixing colors in Blender, and he came up with a simpler way to do it in the slicer. Snapmaker immediately hired him to lead a development team for its fork of OrcaSlicer.

Amazingly, Full Spectrum went from an experimental slicer hack to a must-have for every tool changer in the space of nine months. Snapmaker’s Full Spectrum is tailored for the U1 on open-source OrcaSlicer, while Bambu Lab installed a “Color Mixing” tool in Bambu Studio and Prusa Research developed their own “ColorMix” technology based on hex codes.

Full Spectrum and similar tools can be used on any multimaterial 3D printer. However, because it looks best with super thin layers, tool changers are more efficient and less wasteful.

Snapmaker has since introduced a Full Spectrum filament bundle optimized for four-color machines: a CMYW for lighter, bright colors and a CMYG (gray edition) for darker shades. Ratdoux said the secret is in the filament’s light Transmission Distance (TD), which measures how translucent the material is. Colors that allow more light to pass through them create a better illusion of blending. The parrot and fox pictured above were printed using CMYG and a .08mm layer height. There was no orange, purple, green or black filament used in those prints.

We also found Axiloop, an eight-color tool changer that’s already raised over $700,000 on Kickstarter. The fully enclosed CoreXY machine has a 300x300mm build plate, 4-second tool swaps, and claims to have “near-zero” wipe-free tool changes. Its price for the MC8 Pro is $1,499 for early backers, while the open frame MC8 is $1,099.

Our review unit arrived while I was at Formnext, so I’m excited to put it to the test soon.

Peopoly’s Giga 800 is a large-scale pellet feeder that’s a bit north of our normal prosumer range at $15,000, but I felt it was worth mentioning because it's from our friends at Siraya Tech, who make superior filaments and resin. I noticed quite a few YouTubers happily climb into the machine to show how big it truly is.

The machine has an extrusion output of three kilos an HOUR, which would be equivalent to three spools of normal filament, and can use a 3mm nozzle for chonky prints. We’ve reviewed a similar-sized open-frame “giga” machine before, so I know that being hampered by a normal .4mm nozzle is not something you want with a print volume this large. The enclosed machine is capable of running everything from PLA and TPU to PET-CF and PPA-GF.

Creality had quite a few machines out, but the most interesting were the Creality Falcon T1 UV Laser we reviewed this summer and the new Falcon A1C portable laser we’ll be reviewing soon. The T1 is able to do inner engraving in glass in just a few minutes, and the team was happy to show me the workflow after I supplied them with a photo. They took my selfie, ran it through Creality’s AI to create a 3D bust, then zapped it into a 2 x 3 inch chunk of glass. It was an impressive demo.

They also showed off several handheld scanners, which Creality feels will enable makers to create more practical prints without needing a ton of CAD skills. My favorite is the Creality Pika we reviewed in October.

I’m also particularly intrigued by the mBox kid printer, with a small 153x153mm build plate but lots of safety features to make it child-friendly. The printer is priced at $329, which isn’t bad for a full-feature printer. However, good luck finding one to buy: this printer is only available on the TikTok Shop in the US until December 10.

Another disappointment was the Creality M1 filament maker with its companion R1 shredder. The unit was on display, but not running, which makes me believe they haven’t quite figured out how to make the dream of home filament making a reality.

Elegoo surprised us all with the Centauri X Ultra, a four-color tool changer variation of the wildly successful Centauri Carbon. The Centauri X Ultra is scheduled to release early in 2027. It has a 256x256mm bed, making it the same size as its siblings. The machine is completely enclosed and cleverly contains the side-mounted spools in a Tupperware-like sealed box. The machine has filament drying and a nozzle that can hit 350C, making it a good candidate for high-temperature filaments. It also claims to have 5-second color swaps without waste, but we’ll test that as soon as we get our hands on one.

FlashForge revealed its CJ270 full-color 3D printer, priced at $ 3,999 and now shipping. It is listed as a MultiJet Printer, which uses UV ink to build up models, with a build size of 180 x 120 x 100 mm. Unlike other UV printers, the CJ270 has seven printheads (one for each ink channel), so if one gets clogged, you don’t need to replace the entire printhead. It uses CMYK ink, plus white, clear, and a water-washable support material. The sample models shown were impressive, with lots of detail and strong color.

Anycubic didn’t have any new machines to show off, but they did have a huge announcement to make: they are collaborating with Thingiverse to bring millions of models into Anycubic’s file-sharing library, MakerOnline. Select designs will be converted into multicolor models for one-click printing from Anycubic’s mobile app.

The company is also looking into adding an AI tool dubbed AnyLab to its website to help users create their own designs.

#10272. Why your boss can basically fire you for anything—and why it’s not like that outside the U.S.

We’ve all seen the scene play out in media: A character stands up at work, dramatically declares they quit, and walks out of the office for the last time. While many people will surely empathize with that desire, the reason why a sudden resignation is possible in the U.S. isn’t as great as such a display makes it out to be. 

Mostly because it goes both ways: an employer can axe you at the drop of a hat, in theory—even without a warning, PIP, or other chance to improve.

The U.S. has something called at-will employment, which means that you can leave—or lose—your job without giving any notice.

A job that’s at-will “can end at any moment, for good reason, bad reason, or no reason at all, and with no procedural mandates,” says Gali Racabi, an assistant professor at Cornell’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations and an associated faculty member of Cornell Law School. 

Currently, at-will employment is the law of the land in Washington, D.C., and every U.S. state except Montana. 

“This makes work in the US really easy to sever,” Racabi says.

He adds: “The at-will rule is a travesty, and a mark of moral flaw in our economic order. We need to do away with it ASAP.” 

Critiques of at-will employment

Despite being the default in America—a country whose culture is associated with entrepreneurialism, independence and one that favors employers without much safety-net protection for workers—at-will employment causes a number of concerns. 

Most prominent, perhaps, is a person suddenly losing their income and the many repercussions that can come with that. The practice is also especially risky in the U.S., where individuals often rely on their job for necessary benefits like healthcare—something many other nations provide outside of employment, Racabi says. Say, for instance, a person has an operation scheduled for next week and gets laid off today. Suddenly, they don’t have coverage for a necessary procedure. 

That’s a more extreme example. But even losing health insurance without a big medical issue coming up, and no time to find an alternative, can have devastating repercussions around the cost of medicine, seeing a doctor, or having security in an emergency. 

At-will employment can also complicate the process of proving retaliation or discrimination as the reason for a layoff. 

“Having the at-will rule also makes it really difficult to enforce other work-related laws, like anti-discrimination law,” says Racabi. “If an employer can simply terminate someone without notice, reason, or hearing, it makes proving discriminatory intent extremely hard.” The employer doesn’t have to prove any other justification for the firing.

In a 2022 survey from the National Employment Law Project, 69% of U.S. workers who had experienced a layoff or firing reported that they were either given no or an unfair reason. On top of that, 72% of these participants reported being terminated without a chance to improve or any warning. Overall, 66% of workers surveyed said they support the enactment of just-cause policies. 

Of course, not everyone thinks at-will employment should be thrown out. Carson Young, an associate professor at West Virginia University’s John Chambers College of Business and Economics, argues that at-will employment is “complicated.” It can allow workers to earn higher salaries and have more flexibility than with a just cause system, since the setup potentially lowers employer costs around hiring extra people, with less incentive to keep anyone onboard. 

Young also believes that at-will employment grants workers more freedom to leave a job as they please. He also argues that it could also make employers more likely to hire new employees, as they don’t have to make as big of a commitment to the employee if it ends up not being a good fit, a project ends, or the thing they were hired for doesn’t work out. 

“Employers in [countries] with more job protections are thus more reluctant to hire, because they face greater costs if the hire doesn’t work out,” Young says. 

How the U.S. compares to other countries

The U.S. is fairly unique in having at-will employment, with many other developed countries requiring just cause and notice to terminate an employee. In turn, the individual is often also required to provide notice when leaving a position.

“U.S. courts tend to favor freedom of contract and employer-employee flexibility over job security,” says Young. But “employment law in most other countries places a greater emphasis on job security over freedom of contract and flexibility.”

In the U.K., arguably the country most directly compared to the U.S., an employer can only let you go for “a valid reason that they can justify” and if they’ve “acted reasonably in the circumstance.” An employer will also typically have to give notice of a layoff between one to 12 weeks prior to termination, depending on the length of employment. An employee must give at least a week’s notice, but it can be longer depending on their contract. 

Yet, the U.K. also has zero-hour contracts—which mean an employer doesn’t have to guarantee any work and the individual, in turn, doesn’t have to accept any. These casual contracts are common in positions such as retail or hospitality. 

Critics of the U.K.’s zero-hour contracts point to issues similar to that of at-will employment: Workers on zero-hour contracts “will find it difficult to plan their ordinary lives and pay their bills because they are guaranteed no shifts and will find they have no regular or fixed income stream,” says David Cabrelli, a professor of labor law at the University of Edinburgh’s Law School. 

“Seen from the perspective of job and earnings security, both employment-at-will and zero-hours contracts put workers in a very vulnerable and precarious position.”

Could the U.S. get rid of at-will employment?

The U.K.’s Employment Rights Act 2025 has set new regulations for zero-hour contracts, including a right to guaranteed hours and pay for last-minute shift cancellations. The changes have not yet rolled out, with some employers and unions criticizing the new measures, the Guardian reports. 

Generally, the U.S. is not typically seen as a country that strongly values workers’ rights, instead valuing the good of the employer or business. But could the U.S. also pursue changes? 

Some caveats already exist in circumstances such as whistle-blowing or alleging sexual harassment. “However, these exceptions are issue-specific and the legal position could be improved for workers by the introduction of a just cause dismissal regime,” says Cabrelli. 

So, then, could just cause ever become the law of the land in the U.S.—a place where workers’ rights are rarely prioritized? 

“At-will is law, and we can change laws,” says Racabi. “We can enact statutory just-cause or procedural mandate laws at the federal, state, and local levels. We can do those without significant legal pushback. 

Racabi continues: “We can also support unionization; that one of its byproducts is increased workers’ protection via collective bargaining agreements.” 

At-will employment might be the norm in the U.S., but that doesn’t mean it’s the best option. Or that it has to be around forever.

#10271. This Fitbit Air app buzzes your wrist with phone notifications, finds a lost tracker, more

Google’s Fitbit Air is a simple screenless fitness tracker, but it can do a bit more, and now someone has built an app that lets the Air buzz your wrist when phone notifications come through.

The era of vibe-coding has been very quickly bringing ideas to reality, and these new Fitbit Air notification apps are a great example.

“Air Relay” is the result of a developer managing to reverse-engineer a way to control haptics on the Fitbit Air via Bluetooth without affecting Google Health sync. “Cuff” uses the same method while also showing health stats if you don’t want to use Google Health.

The idea here is pretty simple. You can have apps on your phone ping your Fitbit Air as you choose. “Air Relay” lets you pick select apps and even change the vibration pattern or strength based on the app. You can set “Quiet hours” to prevent notifications while you’re sleeping, and there’s a WhatsApp-specific setting that lets you only get notifications from specific groups or people. A “Find My Air” setting uses Bluetooth strength you help you track down a lost tracker.

While a big part of the appeal of Fitbit Air is its screenless, disconnected nature, having the option to set up alerts for important apps or contacts is certainly a useful option.

“Air Relay” is free on Google Play, and Fitbit Air is available for $99.

#10270. Utah asks to drop criminal charges against Kalshi and its founders

Utah asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, citing Kalshi’s decision to halt trading in the state that had accused it of running an illegal gambling enterprise.

The one-sentence motion filed Tuesday in a Salt Lake City-based court by state Attorney General Derek Brown referenced a “change in circumstance.” Brown’s office noted that it could refile the case if Kalshi resumes offering trades on its platform there.

“Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges,” Brown said in a statement.

Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across more than 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the U.S. Supreme Court.

The felony charges filed by Utah include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.

The state’s charging documents name Kalshi and its cofounders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara. They are due in court in Salt Lake City on December 4, unless a judge agrees to dismiss the case.

Utah law prohibits gambling, and Utah considers prediction markets gambling, Brown’s office said. Many other states contend that the platforms’ sports trading activities are flouting their laws that regulate sports betting and casino gambling.

Utah’s felony charges represented a new tactic in how states are trying to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity. Brown’s office also has asked a court to make Kalshi give up the profits it made in Utah.

Kalshi, the nation’s largest prediction market operator, said Monday it had halted trading in Utah after it became clear that a federal judge hearing a case brought by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) wouldn’t immediately stop Utah’s attempts to shut it down there.

A Kalshi spokeswoman called it an “unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi” but said the company will continue to fight in court for the right to operate in Utah.

Kalshi, like the CFTC, argues that prediction markets offer “event contracts” that should be considered swaps under a federal law that grants exclusive regulation to the federal agency. Utah and at least 44 other states have opposed that view.

Kalshi sued Utah in February, asking a federal judge to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling restrictions on the platform. A federal judge rejected the request, and an appeal is pending.

Trading activity on Kalshi is halted in Nevada and partially in Michigan and Washington, according to Kalshi.

—By Marc Levy, Associated Press

Statement on Jensen Huang's Reinstatement at NVIDIA Chairmen John Moolenaar (R-MI) of the Select Committee on China, Rick Crawford (R-AR) of the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, and Brian Mast (R-FL) of the Foreign Affairs Committee jointly released the following statement concerning Jensen Huang's reinstatement by NVIDIA’s board: “The NVIDIA board’s brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed. The chairpersons of the House Committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence first called upon the Nvidia CEO on November 7 for a closed-door meeting to discuss the allegations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, which lawmakers say “raise significant national security concerns.” Just a day later, Jensen admitted to having an affair, although he did not mention the name of the third party. On the same day that the Nvidia board reinstated Mr. Huang, Senate Banking Committee Chairperson Tim Scott said that Jensen will appear before the committee and publicly testify during a hearing about U.S. export controls on advanced AI hardware.

One of the biggest issues that Jensen Huang is facing is the numerous reports of chip diversion involving Nvidia’s products. The U.S. first put export controls on Nvidia H100 chips in 2022 as it feared that China was using it for military purposes. However, there have been rumors that you could easily get these chips in China as long as you know who to ask as early as 2023, even though the Nvidia CEO answered, “There’s no evidence of any chip diversion,” when asked about it one time. Furthermore, Alice Huang, one of the people that he had an affair with, was allegedly instrumental in securing over $7.5 billion worth of illicit Nvidia GPU imports to China. Jensen Huang himself is known to be against export controls and has called them a failure.

The Select Committee on China’s meeting with the Nvidia CEO will be conducted privately. Although there is going to be a transcription of the interview, it’s unclear if and when the data will be released publicly. On the other hand, the Senate Banking Committee hearing is open to the public and will be broadcast live and online, which will also be the first time that Jensen Huang will face a formal congressional hearing.

#10267. Running an AI Agent on a Local LLM: What I Measured on One GPU

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Running an AI agent on your own GPU sounds simple: point it at Ollama and stop paying per token. I set up OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant, with a 9B model in Ollama on one RTX 3090 and connected it to Discord. Then I read the Ollama log for every request.

The agent worked. The numbers were not what I expected, though. A one-line question turned into a prompt of more than 18,000 tokens, the first reply took over a minute, and the small model sometimes guessed instead of using its tools.

This article covers what I measured and what each number means if you plan to run an agent on local hardware.

OpenClaw ran in Docker and reached Ollama on the host at http://host.docker.internal:11434. Discord was the chat interface, and OpenClaw's web panel showed the sessions and context use.

This article is about the results, not the installation. The full step-by-step setup is in a separate guide to running OpenClaw in Docker with Ollama and Discord. That guide covers the Compose file, the Discord bot and how to keep the ports off your network.

All timings below come from the Ollama log on the test machine. Ollama loaded the model with a 32,768-token context.

My first message in Discord was short: "Which model are you running on, and what is 17 * 23?" The bot answered correctly: it ran on ollama/qwen3.5:9b, and 17 × 23 is 391.

The Ollama log showed what that question cost. The model processed 18,415 prompt tokens and generated 33 tokens.

The extra tokens come from the agent itself. With every request, OpenClaw sends:

On the RTX 3090, reading that prompt took 10 seconds at 1,838 tokens per second. A slower GPU, or a CPU, needs much longer to read the same prompt.

Prompt tokens per model call, from the Ollama log. Only the first message had to process the whole prompt.

OpenClaw counts tokens with its own estimate, which was higher than the Ollama count. The gateway log estimated the prompt at 24,608 tokens, against a prompt budget of 24,576 tokens for this model. By OpenClaw's own count, the base prompt alone used up the budget before any conversation history.

The web panel showed a similar figure: 68 to 69 percent of the context window was in use for the Discord sessions after only a few messages.

The first message arrived while the model was not loaded in GPU memory. That reply took 1 min 10 s:

Reply times on the test machine. Loading the model took most of the first reply.

The speed-up comes from prompt caching. The system prompt, tool definitions and workspace files at the start of the prompt stay the same between requests. Ollama kept that part cached and processed only the new tokens. The model wrote at 91 to 96 tokens per second in every test.

Ollama's documentation says models stay in memory for 5 minutes by default before they are unloaded. After that, the next message pays the load time again. You can change this with the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE environment variable on the Ollama server, or with the keep_alive parameter per request. A negative value, such as -1, keeps the model loaded. I did not change this setting in the test.

If you run Ollama in Docker, pass the variable with -e OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1 or in the environment: section of your Compose file.

Two things used the GPU besides my chat messages.

A heartbeat. OpenClaw's web panel listed one scheduled automation, heartbeat-main, which runs every 30 minutes. The agent wakes on that schedule, so the model gets called even when nobody chats. With Ollama's 5-minute default, the model is unloaded between heartbeats unless someone chatted recently, so a heartbeat most likely starts with a model load. I did not measure this.

An embedding model. During the first message, OpenClaw also called Ollama's /api/embed endpoint twice to index its memory. It used qwen3-embedding:4b, which was already installed on the Ollama server. I did not set OpenClaw to use that model; it picked it on its own.

The two models took this much GPU memory:

That is 11.4 GB for the models alone, almost half of the RTX 3090's 24 GB.

What this means for you: plan GPU memory for the chat model, the embedding model and the context, not the chat model alone. If the GPU also runs other models, the heartbeat can compete with them.

The first two tests in Discord: a question, then a file written with a tool. The user name is blurred.

The mistakes showed up when the model had to check something:

After the restart, the bot claimed it had lost the earlier session. When asked to use its read tool, it read the file correctly.

The fix for the first problem was simple. When I wrote "use your read tool to open homelab-test.md", the model opened the file and listed all three points correctly. Naming the tool made it check instead of guess.

The model listed four files and missed the test file and a folder, because it answered from its prompt.

Based on this test, a local 9B model on one consumer GPU works for:

If you need better answers, OpenClaw also works with hosted models, but then your prompts leave your machine.

In this test, qwen3.5:9b used 6.3 GB and the qwen3-embedding:4b memory model used 5.1 GB. Together the two models needed 11.4 GB.

The model had to load into GPU memory first, which took 59 seconds of the 70-second reply. Ollama keeps a model loaded for 5 minutes by default, and the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE setting changes that.

Every request includes OpenClaw's system prompt, its tool definitions and its workspace files. A one-line question became an 18,415-token prompt in this test.

Yes. A heartbeat automation runs every 30 minutes and calls the model even when nobody sends a message.

It handled questions, arithmetic and file creation correctly in this test. It sometimes answered from its prompt instead of using its tools. When it wrongly said its memory was lost, asking it to use its read tool made it check the file and answer correctly.

#10265. Elon Musk once again promises Tesla’s new autonomous driving is better than humans

Elon Musk has a new promise: Version 15 of Full Self-Driving drives better than a real driver. “Completely new architecture that deserves being called ‘super’ intelligence, as it drives better than human intelligence,” he wrote on X after Tesla started sending the update to a first batch of owners.

That’s great news.

It was great news back in November 2023, too, when he wrote: “Over time, Version 12 (end-to-end neural nets) will far exceed human safety even when unsupervised.” Also in August 2025, when he said: “v14 will be better than human for sure, but I don’t know if it will be 10X. Maybe 2X to 3X. v15 has a shot at 10X.” Back then, he offered no data, and no third-party study to support his claim. It’s the same thing now.

Tesla says that the new FSD v15—which Musk expects to roll out widely in December—upgrades the neural network that processes the camera sensors into information for the car to drive. It has also swapped the old lo-fi grayscale schematic 3D view for an AI-generated live street scene that looks GTA VI-ish. The latter is the only thing that we know is real—and I have to admit it looks pretty neat—but nobody knows if the new driving engine works as well as Musk claims.

Same song, new version number

It may not matter too much. The new v15 is still Level 2 autonomous driving, which means drivers will need to watch the road at all times. While Musk says it drives better than a human, it must be a very dumb human because Tesla’s own support page says the software “does not make the vehicle autonomous” and is meant for use “only with a fully attentive driver.” That matters because when a person has to be ready to take over the wheel at any second, every avoided crash is just as much a win for the human as for the machine.

Tesla claims that the new FSD offers “25x better handling of safety critical cases.” Better than what? Phil Duan, who leads self-driving at Tesla, said on X that “v15 is 25x safer than v14 across the fleet.” Musk answered an X user, too: “Some people thought we meant 25% improvement; no we mean 25 times!” But we don’t really know about how much “safer” v14 was either. As electric mobility site Electrek points out, without real published figures or a peer-reviewed study—like this one on Waymo reducing its crashes with injured people by 85%—that “25x” claim is hard to substantiate.

In a post, the company explains that its new vision encoder—the part of the network that interprets the information from the car’s video cameras—is the reason for that “25x better handling.” Now shared by FSD, Robotaxis, and Optimus humanoids, the engineering team says the new software improves “the critical intervention rate by 25x.” Tesla says the new encoder was trained on “millions of internet videos.”

According to Tesla, v15 adjusts its speed better in bad weather and school zones, steers clear of deep standing water, and is quicker to spot signs, potholes, small animals, chains, and junk on the road. It doesn’t say anything about fake Looney Tunes-painted tunnels.

It can ease off for speed cameras, too. And it learns from you, so if you cancel the slowdown at the same speed camera twice, by accelerating, it will stop braking at that point of the road. The company also claims that the car’s interior camera—which checks if you are paying attention to the road or not—now works more often when you wear hats and sunglasses.

Neat!

As part of the update, Tesla Reality View has changed. It now looks very similar to the live situational awareness screens you get in some Chinese cars: a hyperrealistic view of the road and your car as seen from behind at a 45-degree angle. You can see vehicles and people in 3D hyperrealistic renderings. Even the buildings are textured and lit like the real thing. It feels like a high-end car racing game. Musk claims “it’s like GTA.”

It looks neat, but it doesn’t seem to convey information better than the older user interface (UI), which showed a much clearer representation of reality. Seen from a high angle, it was a simplified, very stylized version of the road populated with semitransparent versions of vehicles and nearby people. In the old version, despite its perception problems, it was easy to get instant situational awareness. In the new v15, the realism obscures the information with too much darkness and glitz.

The interface also features a blue ribbon that traces the route FSD intends to drive, so you can correct it. Chevron arrows float overhead before every turn. And the map now shows several parking spots at your destination. Some Chinese car manufacturers are already displaying this information directly on the windshield, projecting computer-generated wide-screen augmented-reality (AR) graphics over the real world.

Fortunately, you can switch to a split view or just pick the GPS map view. Musk claims “you can tap any point on the reality revisualizer to make your car go there.” 

Musk says that the new UI uses the same visual features the FSD v15 driving model uses: It’s all AI-generated. The AI model renders short bursts of eight frames at 36 frames per second, using just half of one of the accelerators in the car’s AI4 computer.

Still, the video may lag behind reality because the AI is not fast enough. Musk admits the lag is “a bit high due to compute constraints.” He claims Tesla has a way to trim it by about 35%. More promises.

If December’s wide release arrives on time (which may or may not happen), it will put the new FSD in a lot more hands. In 2027 we will be able to test the real value of Musk’s promises once again. Let’s stay positive. Maybe this will be it. You know what they say: 15th time’s the charm.

#10262. How Nvidia employees feel about Jensen Huang’s return

The public reaction to Jensen Huang’s return has been mixed at best, raising the hackles of lawmakers and corporate governance experts. Even the stock price took a bit of a dip after surging by over 30% on Monday. Within the company, however, the mood appears to be considerably lighter. 

In videos that are circulating across social media, Huang received a hero’s welcome at Nvidia headquarters, where his employees lined the walls cheering for him. Between chants of “Jensen! Jensen!” and “We love you, Jensen,” he addressed his staff in a display of contrition. 

“I’m terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this,” he said. “I’ve made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” After an employee threw her arms around Huang in a tight hug—lasting over 10 seconds—he continued: “Thank you all for the second chance. I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”

Many Nvidia employees have taken to LinkedIn to express their relief over Huang’s return, seemingly overlooking the indiscretions that led to his ousting. They heaped praise on their newly reinstated CEO, describing him as the “heartbeat of Nvidia” and “one of a kind.” 

One employee even invoked Charles Dickens, paraphrasing the opening of A Tale of Two Cities: “It was the worst of times, it is the best of times. It was the season of Darkness, it is the season of Light. It was the winter of despair, it is the spring of hope. We had nothing before us, we have everything before us.”

Another employee claimed he always knew Huang would return to Nvidia: “When Jensen stepped down, many said their goodbyes and thanked him for his legacy. I stayed quiet—not out of indifference, but because deep down I knew there is only one boss, and he would be back.”

A former robotics engineer at Nvidia—who quit rather publicly after Huang’s resignation—congratulated him on X and admitted he made a hasty decision. “Looking back, I may have moved too quickly, and I don’t want to rush into another major decision. For now, I’d like to take some time to rest, reflect, and think carefully about my future. As part of that, I’m open to exploring the possibility of returning.”

These reactions line up with previous reports about employee sentiment after Huang stepped down: According to Wired, many employees showed immediate support for him internally, asking the board to reverse the decision. More than 10,000 current Nvidia employees, or about a quarter of its workforce, signed a petition to reinstate Huang as CEO.

Still, there are some employees who seem to feel differently—perhaps those who have been the target of Huang’s outbursts and creative insults, as reported by The New York Times recently. 

In a Wired report this week, several current and former employees expressed frustration over the turn of events, in part because they had hoped Huang’s exit would usher in some long overdue changes. A number of employees were disturbed by Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy and at least one inappropriate relationship with an employee. 

Beyond that, however, they also felt that Nvidia condoned abusive behavior and echoed previous claims that Huang belittled employees at times. (In an internal post, one employee asserted: “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again.”) Workers also told Wired that the focus on unity and the “one team” ethos discouraged employees from challenging leadership.

Even employees who have few misgivings about the culture may now find themselves questioning Huang’s leadership. One engineering leader openly grappled with his feelings about Huang in a LinkedIn post he shared before the CEO was reinstated. “Some believe his contributions to Nvidia and the industry are so extraordinary that he deserves another chance,” he wrote. “Others argue that making exceptions for powerful leaders sets a dangerous precedent. I’ve wrestled with this question all week. My opinion has probably changed every single day. And I’ve realized something. I don’t have a clear answer.”

As evidenced by the reception to Huang yesterday, this may not be the prevailing view among employees.
