#10258. Americans are sick of disruptive leaders, data shows

Business culture has long lionized bold, disruptive leaders. But these days, at least, Americans are yearning for some stability.   

In a survey conducted shortly after the midterm elections, 82% of Americans said they prefer leaders who “get things back to normal rather than shake things up” and 82% also said they prefer a “stable and predictable” life.

The New York-based global public relations firm Burson interviewed about 1,600 Americans across party lines. The poll was published November 14.

An overwhelming 90% of respondents also said they want honest, calm, consistent leadership, and 75% said they lose respect for CEOs who change positions under pressure.

It is easy to interpret these findings as a reflection of current public opinion about President Donald Trump. Trump’s penchant for disruption and his brash businessman image helped him win the White House twice, but the outcome of the midterms—and the results of the Burson survey—indicate that the public has grown tired of the chaos.

In a separate Associated Press poll, about two-thirds of the roughly 100,000 midterm voters surveyed thought Trump has the wrong priorities, while 7 in 10 said Congress hasn’t been doing enough to check the president’s power.

As Fast Company reported earlier this month, the midterm results also illustrate the risks organizations face when they become overly dependent on a single charismatic leader. Successful leaders can make subordinates increasingly reluctant to question their judgment, even when circumstances change.

“At some point, you have to ask whether people are following your vision, or simply afraid to challenge it,” leadership expert Adam Mendler said.

#10257. Trump is deploying a special ‘Tiger Team’ for Thanksgiving air travel. Here’s why

Recent chaos is making Americans wary of braving air travel this holiday season, but the Trump administration says it has a plan.

The White House recently announced the formation of a “tiger team” dedicated to preventing major mess-ups like the recent multi-hour ground stop, which snarled airports nationwide as a mountain of delayed and rescheduled flights piled up. The mid-November incident lasted more than four hours, grounding planes all over the country as the federal government scrambled to get the standard lines of communications for air traffic controllers back online. 

Trump’s special interagency group known as the “Transportation Technology Transformation Tiger Team” will bring together representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the Department of Transportation, the Department of Defense, and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, according to the White House. “As millions of Americans prepare to travel for the Thanksgiving holiday, President Donald J. Trump is making sure the skies stay open and the systems run smoothly,” the White House said in a press release.

The FAA reported that 12,462 flights were canceled during the ground stop, which began mid-afternoon on Friday, November 13. The FAA is still investigating the technical hiccup that prompted thousands of planes to be grounded, but a routine router upgrade completed by federal contractor L3Harris Technologies in Arkansas is believed to be at fault.

Tiger teams in action

The term “tiger team” is sometimes used in corporate settings, but it is more commonly used to describe small highly skilled teams convened to solve difficult problems in government and military operations. The most famous tiger team in history is credited with guiding NASA’s Apollo 13 mission back to Earth safely, a feat that earned then-Flight Director (and later NASA Mission Operations Director) Gene Kranz and his specialized group a Presidential Medal of Freedom. 

Other U.S. agencies use tiger teams for specialized problem-solving, including the U.S. Department of Labor. The Trump administration appears to have a particular affinity for the term and also formed a self-described tiger team across the Department of Energy and the Department of the Interior last year to “unleash” the American energy industry. That group later became bogged down wrestling with oil prices and inflation tied to the war in Iran.

Aside from its tongue-twister of a name (try saying it five times fast), very little is known about Trump’s Transportation Technology Transformation Tiger Team. A White House official told The Daily Wire that the FAA is looking into “near-term” network configuration options and other short-term ways to boost the stability of current air traffic control systems while slower modernization efforts move forward. 

“President Trump and Secretary Duffy have brought together the best and the brightest across the government to ensure what happened last Friday can never happen again,” White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said. “This team has hit the ground running in modernizing and improving the reliability of the nation’s decades-old air traffic control system.” 

Schuster claimed that American skies are already safer, thanks to the “tremendous progress” from the tiger team, but reassuring Americans skittish about air safety after a spate of recent scares may not be that easy. Modernizing the U.S. air traffic control system is a major long-term goal pursued by multiple administrations and scores of lawmakers. Yet the ground stop showed that pushing technology fixes into an ancient system that never goes offline carries its own set of risks.

Record holiday travel expected

In a press release, the Transportation Department said it expects to see the “busiest holiday skies in 16 years,” with more than 417,000 flights forecast for the nine days beginning on Monday of Thanksgiving week. Tuesday is projected to be the busiest travel day of the period, with more than 52,000 flights scheduled. 

“From standing up a Tiger Team to ensure a seamless travel experience for fliers to using a successful new platform to predict and address congestion in the airspace, we’ve taken unprecedented action to limit flight delays and cancellations,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. “The American people can rest assured we will be on the clock 24/7 to get families to their destinations safely and on time.”

Last month, a former OpenAI employee with ties to Saudi Arabia was arrested for bugging conference rooms in the company. Today, Bloomberg reports that prosecutors in the case uncovered hundreds of recordings, dozens of which were meetings and conversations dating as far back as September. Prosecutors believe some recordings may contain sensitive information that can be regarded as trade secrets, the dispersion of which could be a threat to US national security.

In October, we covered how Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI employee, was arrested for installing a covert listening device behind the company's executive conference room television using a Seeed Xiao ESP32-S3. The device was discovered days later, with investigations linking it to Alfozan and subsequently leading to his arrest and removal from the company.

According to this latest report, prosecutors urged a federal judge to deny Alfozan’s request to be released on bail while the investigation is ongoing, fearing that Alfozan might flee before trial “given his relatively weak ties to the US and the considerable […] connections he has in his native Saudi Arabia.”

Prosecutors have stated, “Thus far, the government has located hundreds of audio files on the defendant’s personal computer, including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, many of which involve discussions of what may be trade secrets,” as reported by Bloomberg. The court filing also says that Alfozan kept audio files and AI-generated transcripts on his computer, with some recordings uploaded to Dropbox, “meticulously categorized by date and renamed according to the content of the recording.” Prosecutors also found a collections of images of a "strategic partnership" document marked as confidential on Alfozan's confiscated phone.

The filing also states, “At the same time as he was secretly recording, cataloging, and transcribing dozens of meetings concerning (among other things) OpenAI’s partnerships and capabilities, the defendant was in frequent communication with various people affiliated with the Saudi government.” However, Alfozan denies stealing trade secrets from OpenAI for Saudi Arabia, with his lawyer arguing that Alfozan “has no special or covert ties to the Saudi government,” in a separate court filing on Friday.

According to the October 27 indictment, he is charged with interception of oral communications, not theft of trade secrets or economic espionage, as with sharing trade secrets with another government. Alfozan requested to set his bond at $1 million, but this could be denied at the hearing set for Tuesday; additional charges could also follow if the investigation finds out what Alfozan is doing, or plans to do, with the recordings and to whom he would send them.

#10253. The Jensen Huang saga poses the question: What happens when a leader becomes too big to fail?

Less than a week after Nvidia’s board said it would not reinstate Jensen Huang, it renamed him president and CEO. President Donald Trump had intervened, showing his support for Huang publicly and reportedly even phoning in to a board meeting, urging Nvidia’s directors to reconsider their position.

While Huang is a visionary leader who has delivered extraordinary results, putting him back at the helm despite an open, independent investigation of his conduct may put the company at even greater risk. How will managers hold their teams accountable if the CEO is perceived to be able to violate the company’s code of conduct and lie about it to the board and employees without repercussions?

As an executive and team coach, I’ve seen this situation time and again (albeit not to this extreme), and it creates a near-impossible situation for the rank and file. Leaders must now hold their teams accountable when employees have reason to question that the minimum standards are discretionary.

Why people defend problematic high performers

Compensation was the most submitted question that then-Interim CEO Colette Kress received during last week’s company-wide meeting. And it makes sense—the stock price dropped sharply when Huang announced his resignation.

Yet it’s not just money that likely motivated more than 1,600 comments on an internal post, most supporting Huang’s return. There is also a sense of pride in being part of a winning team, one that was synonymous with Huang. In many ways, defending him may feel like defending what they’ve helped build.

Moreover, with approximately 60 employees reporting directly to Huang, there is no apparent successor—heightening the business risk of replacing him. That, coupled with external political and investor pressure from heavyweights such as Trump, Elon Musk, and Bill Ackman, likely fueled the sentiment that Huang should be reinstated.

What happens when exceptions become precedents

Employees may trust Huang’s business judgment but question how Nvidia handles misconduct. The implications of the board’s reversal will likely take time to fully materialize. For example, what happens when a less indispensable leader violates company policy, or new allegations emerge against Huang or another executive? Will employees become less willing to raise concerns if consequences depend on someone’s perceived value to the company?

Huang’s personal missteps may also erode trust and credibility with employees, after reports that he misled company leaders about his affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang have shown he is willing to deceive people in his personal and professional life. Employees may think, What else is he capable of? This may affect employees’ willingness to stake their own reputations behind him.

Managers may also struggle to hold employees to certain expectations when those employees believe exceptions can be made.

One client of mine, whom I’ll call Eliza, is a chief revenue officer who worked with an underperforming VP of sales with a long-standing friendship with the company’s CEO. Although the VP of sales did not perform the basic functions of his role, Eliza couldn’t hold him accountable because the CEO would not back her up. She was responsible for the company’s revenue goal without having the authority to deliver it. Ultimately, Eliza gave the CEO an ultimatum: It was either her or the VP. The CEO ended up moving the VP to another department, but the company nearly lost Eliza in the process. 

Managing a double standard

When Huang returned to the office, an employee shouted, “We love you, Jensen!”

And while his return may be welcome to many, it will create a disparity in expectations that managers will have to address. I once worked with a senior executive in a similar situation. His team’s frustration with the CEO’s decisions became all-consuming—and he agreed with them. He spent his nights and weekends agonizing, and he found himself adding to their list of grievances in team meetings.

He felt awful, and so did his team. I told him he had a decision to make. He could continue with the status quo, or he could acknowledge the reality of the situation and decide whether he wanted to stay or leave the company. 

He ultimately decided to look for a new job, but in the interim he focused his team on what they could influence. While he didn’t disclose to his team that he was looking for work elsewhere, he did tell them that while they worked for this company, they were responsible for having productive conversations that moved the business forward. If anyone felt they couldn’t do that, he would support them if they decided to leave. This alleviated the burden he felt he was carrying by trying to “protect” his team. 

Managers who are in the thankless position of serving under a divisive leader are stuck between a rock and a hard place. They are caught between a leader they can’t remove and their employees. Their best bet is to be clear about where their authority begins and ends, and make it clear that their team, including themselves, will be held to a high standard. But the internal cost of doing this when the company’s leader is not held to the same standard is high; it creates a ripe breeding ground for talented managers and employees to leave.

While it is rare for a company to be ensnared in a scandal of this magnitude, leaders often face pressure to overlook the behavior of someone who delivers exceptional results. Overlooking this behavior may seem like the easiest path for continuing to deliver exceptional results—but it comes with a cost: the well-being of the rest of the team. This is why adequate succession planning is so critical, so no one becomes “too big to fail.”

#10252. Best Ecommerce Platforms for Developers: Six Options and the Layers Each Leaves You

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

Shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that plan. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide shows how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

WooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

BigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the company says you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

#10251. Billy Evans may have gotten a share of the profits from ‘You Can See Everything’ after all

You Can See Everything may begin as a documentary about disgraced tech entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes in the month before her prison sentence, but in the movie’s second half, an entirely different (and entirely meta) subject emerges: the deal between Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, and studio A24 to give Evans a cut of the film’s profits, and codirector Nathan Fielder’s uncertainty about how much Holmes knows about the money.

Given Evans’s status as the film’s quasi-villain, the thought that ticket buyers’ money would end up in his pockets had moviegoers squirming in their seats. Thankfully, the documentary ends with a title card saying that Evans “decided to give up his right to profit on the movie” shortly after filming concluded. 

But a new investigation says that Evans didn’t fully forgo his payout from the film—it was just redirected to charity instead.

Evans’s share of the profits

Two anonymous sources told The Hollywood Reporter that Evans and A24 amended their agreement so his payout would go to an unnamed children’s charity, not directly into his bank account. An A24 representative later confirmed that this deal was made, though they didn’t say why that detail was omitted from the film’s final title card.

The exact size of Evans’s payout remains unknown, but given You Can See Everything’s unprecedented success at the box office, his share is definitely more than small change. This week, the film crossed $100 million in global box-office revenue, making it the fifth-highest-grossing non-concert documentary of all time.

In a separate interview for THR, Evans explained why he agreed to back out on his initial deal with A24.

“They said that it would help the project. Time and time again, when there’s things that I really didn’t want to do that they said would be helpful for making a better movie and helping people see Liz more clearly, I made those sacrifices or decisions to help the project,” Evans said. “I am totally stubborn, but if there’s anything that I can do to help Liz regardless of the cost, I will do it.”

Why the directors disagree

Though THR’s report frames You Can See Everything’s final title card as disingenuous, directors Fielder and Lance Oppenheim say the outlet’s story misses the mark.

At a Q&A on November 21, Fielder and Oppenheim reportedly said the story’s wording was inaccurate and that none of the documentary’s subjects were paid, according to reporting by Semafor.

A studio source later told Semafor that Evans fully relinquished his profit-sharing deal, and that the charitable donation was a separate, mutual agreement between Evans and A24.

Meanwhile, THR’s editor-in-chief, Maer Roshan, defended the story over email, saying that A24’s perspective “seems like a pretty semantic argument.”

#10247. AI can help moms. It can’t replace the village

Susan (pseudonym) regularly goes to AI for parenting help. When her child is sick, she checks whether she needs to call the doctor. When her toddler is acting out, she looks to AI to find out if it’s normal. But then, she takes the question to her online parenting group at Peanut to double-check.

She already has an answer. So what is she still looking for?

AI is always there. When we have a question at 2 a.m. and no one else is awake, we can ask Claude. When we fear judgment, ChatGPT will almost always validate. Is AI going to replace the “parenting village” we were all supposed to find?

Maybe, but probably not.

Curious about how this is all playing out, I went looking for answers in a few places. I started with Michele Battersby, president of Peanut, an online community platform for mothers. Her team looked at public conversations on the platform mentioning AI over 90 days. Mothers were asking about everything: health, development, sleep, feeding, and all the life logistics that go with parenting.

But while they were asking these questions, it seems AI was often just a starting place. AI can give us information. It can be a place to ask a question that we might otherwise feel embarrassment about. It can even help with the mental load (more on that later). But even with all of that, mothers on the app were still going to other mothers for support and to talk about their actual experiences.

Because sometimes we’re looking for more than an answer.

I’ve been thinking about this as AI becomes part of what we’re calling the parenting village. I recently asked my LinkedIn community whether they were using AI for parenting support. Of 133 people who responded, 30% said they regularly used it for the mental load, 21% regularly used it for parenting questions, 20% used it sometimes or rarely, and 28% weren’t using it for parenting at all.

It’s a small, self-selected poll, but the conversations were interesting. Some women talked about how much AI was helping them. Others worried about what we might lose if we started turning to technology instead of each other.

Both things are probably true.

But perhaps the bigger question is this: Are we creating a world where mothers have more kinds of support, or one where we’re asking technology to compensate for the human and institutional support that’s missing?

Because filling those gaps doesn’t negate the need to fix what created them in the first place.

Why mothers are turning to AI

The Surgeon General’s 2024 advisory on parental mental health found that 48% of parents reported feeling completely overwhelmed by stress on most days, compared with 26% of other adults. 

And mothers are bearing a disproportionate share of the work. A 2025 study of 2,133 partnered American parents found that as women’s employment and earnings increased, their physical household labor decreased, but their cognitive labor didn’t decrease in the same way.

Parents are stressed, and mothers are carrying an enormous burden without enough support. So it makes sense to me that they’re looking for help wherever they can find it.

The mental load seems like an easy place to start. The New York Times recently wrote about AI family assistants that help parents manage school emails, calendars, and household schedules. And in a 2026 survey from Lurie Children’s Hospital, about two-thirds of parents said AI had reduced their mental load. Parents reported saving an average of 58 minutes a week, and 91% said using AI increased their confidence as parents.

If something can help with all those logistics, why not let it?

The appeal of AI goes beyond organizing the family calendar.

Motherhood is rife with judgment everywhere you look. Something as simple as diapers can become some sort of moral crisis. And let’s not get started on how we feed or discipline our children.

Reaching out with questions as a mom can feel terrifying with good reason. When I was a new mother, I remember trying to get advice about breastfeeding and returning to work. I was struggling to figure out how to keep my milk supply up, and I turned to an online parenting group hoping for some practical help. Instead, I was essentially told that if I wanted to breastfeed, I shouldn’t be working. It was devastating.

AI has an obvious appeal. It’s available, and it doesn’t judge.

That can be valuable, but it’s not the same thing as having support from another person.

We still need the village 

AI can validate, but it can’t coregulate with us in the way another person can. It can’t feel with us or share its own vulnerability. And especially when it comes to parenting, human connection is an undervalued part of the village. 

We think we’re looking for an answer, but what we also need is to hear from another person who has been through something similar, who can tell us what it was like for them, or admit that they struggled, too.

Of course, that doesn’t always happen. Other people can be judgmental. They can give us advice we didn’t ask for. They can misunderstand what we’re going through. Yet when we do find someone who understands, there’s something different about that experience.

Emerging research sheds some potential light on this, too. A 2026 study in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology found that college students who interacted regularly with another student over two weeks experienced greater reductions in loneliness than those interacting with a supportive AI chatbot.

Meanwhile, another study comparing perceptions of AI companions with support from friends and family found that young adults who reported stronger support from the humans in their lives were less likely to view AI companionship favorably.

Neither study was about mothers, and the second doesn’t establish cause and effect. But I find that really important; it raises the possibility that AI becomes more appealing when we don’t have the human support we need.

AI can fill in where we have holes in the village, but it’s not a replacement for the people who understand what we’re going through.

What happened to the village?

But what about this mythical village?

You know, the group of mom friends who all have kids the same age, who parent the same way we do, who are always there when we need them. We’re supposed to find these people, become best friends, and have this amazing support system.

Maybe we even all move into a commune together and live happily ever after.

But I don’t know that I’ve ever really seen that village exist in quite the way we imagine it. And I wonder if part of the problem is that we’re thinking about the village too narrowly.

When we talk about finding our village, we’re usually talking about the social village. Friends, other parents, extended family, and the people who understand what we’re going through. However, too often, finding a social village can feel like another item on an overflowing to-do list.

Instead of telling mothers to try harder to find their people, we need to make it easier for those connections to happen.

I recently joined Fast Company‘s M Suite, a community for working mothers, and was struck by how quickly I felt connected to women I’d never met. Women who were thinking about the same questions of ambition, careers, motherhood, caregiving, and identity. And I found myself wanting to meet some of them in person.

Peanut’s 2026 Motherhood Index found that conversations about friendship and community increased 82% year over year, while conversations about offline meetups and playdates increased 53%. Those numbers reflect changes in conversations on Peanut, not necessarily changes in how all mothers are feeling. But I think they’re interesting, particularly the growing interest in meeting offline.

In response, Peanut is also helping mothers make those connections happen. Its Village Fund, in partnership with Coterie, a maker of hypoallergenic diapers, provides grants to mothers who want to organize gatherings. In funding in-person experiences, it’s making the social village more accessible.

But there’s also what I think of as the structural village. Affordable childcare that actually has openings, paid leave, workplace flexibility, community resources, and help at home with the tangible work of parenting.

The support AI can’t provide

There’s a difference between adding AI to our village and expecting it to make up for everything that’s missing. we are now telling moms, “Go to AI,” but that doesn’t mean AI can replace help at home, help at work, or government policies around childcare and paid leave.

A 2026 Pew Research Center study found that 71% of working parents said having flexibility over their working hours would be highly helpful, but only 25% actually had substantial flexibility. And according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, only 49% of private sector workers had access to paid family and medical leave in 2026.

Meanwhile, even in families where both parents work, mothers are far more likely to be the primary caregivers. Federal Reserve data found that 49% of mothers in dual-earner couples said they were usually responsible for caring for their children when they were home, compared with just 8% of fathers (the remaining 43% said they shared childcare equally).

These aren’t problems we can solve by becoming better organized, and they’re not problems AI can prevent or solve for us.

AI can help with some of the mental load. But why is so much of that load falling on mothers in the first place? AI can draft us the perfect script to ask for flexibility at work, but that doesn’t mean our workplaces will provide it. AI can help us find all the day cares in our area, but it doesn’t make childcare affordable or available. 

Let’s embrace AI even when it only solves one thing. As mothers we need all the help we can get. But let’s not confuse making an unreasonable amount of responsibility more manageable with actually changing how much responsibility mothers are expected to carry. Because we can’t let AI be the thing that lets the system off the hook.

#10245. I love YouTube on TV, but we desperately need better watchlist controls

Managing a YouTube watchlist shouldn’t be as frustrating as it is, especially on the most-used app in my life. Google’s premier streaming app has too many issues with resurfacing content; in my opinion, this is now a major problem that needs to be fixed.

Aside from my YouTube watchlist gripes, it’s no secret that moving from a web browser to the TV is ultimately still a frustrating experience.

Lots of things I love about watching videos on my laptop or PC just don’t translate well to when I’m sat on my sofa holding a remote trying to find something to watch after wrapping up for the day. One thing I’m getting annoyed with is how YouTube scales on TV and Android TV boxes because you’re given less choice and arguably poorer recommendations for content due to the constraints in place.

Understandably, you can’t compress the layout too much on a TV as you’re typically sat a few feet away and all aspects of the interface need to be legible. I would still like to tweak it, though, if that were possible.

Maybe we could get proper sections for content, like how Netflix and other streaming platforms offer categorized areas where you can search for “comedy” or “horror”. I’m almost certain that, with Google’s insane investment and massive AI push, where every video is already analyzed hundreds of times, that wouldn’t be too difficult to do.

The problem now is that the sidebar menu is just too broad. Gaming covers basically everything. Then each line of videos accounts for one title, but requires search and previous watch data to populate. I find myself often fighting with recommendations on my TV, whereas on desktop it’s not as much of a problem.

That leads me to my biggest problem with YouTube, and it’s the, frankly, embarrassing watchlist or “Watch later” controls.

I can’t fault that it works, but right now the watchlist function is like something out of the early 2000s due to the lack of flexibility that I touched on above. As my YouTube consumption has increased 20x over the past four or five years, managing what I want to come back to or might have missed the first time around is starting to become a bit of a chore.

I’ve tried using playlists to save things, but things get messy very quickly because of how cumbersome it is to a) create a playlist on TV and b) how playlists are organized by default.

Google TV isn’t perfect, but it’s where I keep my biggest TV and movie watchlist outside of YouTube. Yes, YouTube is mostly for user-generated content, but I would take something as basic as Google TV’s interface baked into YouTube somehow. Add in categorization and auto-clear.

The Watch Later section has become an unwieldy place that I never really want to go unless I desperately have to. I’m constantly losing videos that I hoped to come back to or have an affinity for.

Videos don’t clear automatically, nor do you know when they were added. Yes, I’ll give credit that you can sort by a few options, but that’s the bare minimum. The process of moving things around is slow and takes multiple taps. Watch Later is also hidden compared to other services. It’s under your account, then beneath “Liked videos,” which is below any you may have uploaded yourself.

On a TV, the process is so annoying I just avoid it altogether. You go to the sidebar menu > Library > Watch later. It should be front-and-center on a TV. It’s almost unforgivable in my eyes because even your watch history is given greater prominence. I simply cannot understand that decision.

I’m not always a huge fan of AI being shoehorned into apps and services, but this is one of those areas that has been left to rot for a while and could get a big uplift from adding in a little bit of Gemini. Even if it were just an enhanced search function or more tools for organizing.

With YouTube TV effectively taking over regular broadcast television and being the world’s biggest streaming platform, I’m shocked by how so many areas of the platform remain in a consistently neglected state.

A little bit of spit and polish, and maybe I’ll start using this section again. For now, though, I’ll stick to texting myself links of stuff I want to watch. The ball is in your court, Google.

There was once a time when OLED gaming monitors commanded a hefty premium over their IPS- and VA-based competition. However, especially over the past year, prices have dropped low enough that we’re seeing some really compelling prices on OLED monitors. Such is the case for anyone looking to purchase a 27-inch gaming monitor, which you can now find for well under $300. For example, you can get an Acer Predator X27U W1 for $269.99, while the Innocn 2780S is available for $279 at Amazon.

I’ve found a total of four 27-inch QHD monitors that are worth your attention (including the two mentioned above), so without further ado, let's see what’s cooking.

The Acer Predator X27U W1 is a 27-inch gaming monitor with a QHD resolution, 240 Hz refresh rate, and a QD-OLED panel. It supports AMD FreeSync Premium and includes two HDMI 2.1 and two DisplayPort 1.4 ports.

The Acer Predator X27U W1 features a 26.5-inch QD-OLED Penta Tandem panel. Acer claims that the Penta Tandem panel boosts luminous efficiency, doubles panel life, and allows for peak brightness of up to 1,000 nits (although typical brightness is closer to 200 nits).

You’ll find a 240 Hz refresh rate with support for AMD FreeSync Premium, 0.03 ms GtG response time, 99 percent coverage of the sRGB color space, an anti-glare coating over the display panel, and dual 3-watt speakers. On the connectivity front, you get two HDMI 2.1 ports, two DisplayPort 1.4 ports, and a single 3.5 mm headphone jack. The Predator X27U W1 is also adjustable for height, pivot, tilt, and swivel. The monitor rings up with a 14 percent discount at Amazon, bringing its final price to $269.99.

The Innocn 2780S is a 27-inch gaming monitor with a QHD resolution, 240 Hz refresh rate, and a QD-OLED panel. It covers 99% of sRGB and DCI-P3 and offers peak brightness of 400 nits.

The Innocn 2780S follows a similar formula with a matte screen finish, 0.03 ms GtG response time, and 99 percent sRGB coverage (and 99 percent for DCI-P3). However, the monitor doesn’t list any official AMD FreeSync Premium or G-Sync certification, only claiming Adaptive-Sync support from 48 Hz to 240 Hz. Innocn lists brightness for the QD-OLED panel at 250 nits typical and 400 nits peak/HDR. You still get two HDMI 2.1 ports and two DisplayPort 1.4 ports, along with a 3.5 mm headphone jack and two 3-watt speakers. The 2780S is now available at 20 percent off, ringing up at $279.99.

The Gigabyte GO27Q24G switches the formula up slightly, instead opting for a 27-inch Micro Lens Array+ White OLED (MLA+ OLED) display. As the counter to popular QD-OLED panels, WOLED panels tend to be brighter across the operating range. Indeed, Gigabyte states that the GO27Q24G offers a typical brightness of 275 nits and can hit a peak of 1,300 nits with HDR content.

The GO27Q24G is definitely a looker, as it sports a 4-sided borderless design with extremely thin bezels. It also features a RealBlack Glossy, which strikes a good balance between the color-enhancing clarity of a glossy screen coating and the reflection-rejecting characteristics of matte coatings.

The Gigabyte GO27Q24G is a 27-inch gaming monitor with a QHD resolution, 240 Hz refresh rate, and an MLA+ WOLED panel. It features a RealBlack Glossy display, a 4-sided borderless design, and can hit 1,300 nits peak brightness.

The monitor has AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync Compatible certifications, along with a maximum refresh rate of 240 Hz. As for ports, you’ll get two HDMI 2.1, one DisplayPort 1.4, one USB-C, and one 3.5 mm headphone jack. However, one thing you won’t find is integrated speakers.

We recently reviewed the GO27Q24G and came away impressed with its value, video processing, and brightness. As our Christian Eberele explained, “Image and gaming experience are every bit the equal of monitors costing twice as much. The GO27Q24G’s Micro Lens Array delivers tremendous brightness, as much as 1,300 nits in HDR mode. It also has nearly perfect viewing angles. Color volume isn’t quite as large as panels with Quantum Dots or Tandem RGB Stripes, but you do get over 96% coverage of DCI-P3.”

The Gigabyte GO27Q24G is currently on sale for $297.47, representing a 15 percent discount.

The AOC Agon Pro AG276QZD2 is a 27-inch gaming monitor with a QHD resolution, 240 Hz refresh rate, and a QD-OLED panel. It supports AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync and offers a peak brightness of 1,000 nits.

Finally, we have the AOC Agon Pro AG276QZD2, which is another 27-inch QD-OLED monitor that we reviewed nearly two years ago. The monitor supports AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync, and has 250 nits typical brightness (1,000 nits peak). It also comes with two HDMI 2.0 ports, one DisplayPort 1.4 port, and a 3.5 mm headphone jack.

Eberle went on to write about the AG276QZD2, stating, “It has a huge color gamut thanks to Quantum Dot tech, which is larger than last year’s AG276QZD. Accuracy comes from a factory calibration that can only be slightly improved with adjustment. It also delivers the best gaming performance available from any monitor with perfect motion resolution and low input lag.”

If the AOC Agon Pro AG276QZD2 tickles your fancy, you can get it now for $297.49, which is a 15 percent discount.

#10243. Your SSL certificates can now last 200 days at most: The real risk isn’t renewal

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan. Following the latest update from the CA/Browser Forum, the maximum lifetime of a certificate has fallen from 398 days to 200, and it will drop to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Renewal is no longer an annual chore. It’s an ongoing task that only stays manageable with automation.

So what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes? For many setups, very little will change. For others, one missed renewal can mean an outage. This article explains what’s changing and what to do if you’re in the second group.

Today, an SSL certificate is valid for 200 days at most. The limit applies when a certificate is issued, so the ones you already hold keep their original expiration date.

Where you feel it depends on how your certificates renew. Sites on managed hosting platforms or behind a content delivery network (CDN) usually renew automatically already, often every 90 days, so the new limit changes little. The pressure lands on setups where someone buys a certificate once a year and installs it by hand. At 47 days, that becomes about 12 renewals a year.

A certificate is a promise from a certificate authority that a key really belongs to a domain, and that promise gets less reliable the longer it runs. If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, it stays usable until it expires. Cutting the lifetime shrinks that window, so a problem that once lingered for over a year is now fixed in weeks.

Shorter lifetimes also make revocation, the process for canceling a bad certificate, far less critical. Revocation has never worked perfectly, but a certificate that expires within weeks matters much less if a cancellation doesn’t reach every browser.

Another reason is about people. A task done once a year is easy to forget and hard to check from outside. Browser makers have pushed for years to move the industry onto automatic renewal, on the logic that a process that runs every few weeks gets tested constantly. If it breaks, you notice quickly instead of discovering it on the day the certificate expires.

For most people, the first effect is simply more work. A certificate that once needed attention every year will soon need it every few weeks. Plus, each renewal is a small chance for something to go wrong. Multiply that by dozens of sites, mail servers, and devices, and the chance of one slipping through grows quickly.

The safety nets are also thinner. If you relied on the renewal emails, nothing is watching your certificates now. Additionally, with a shorter life, there’s less time between this should have renewed and this has expired.

An expired certificate doesn’t make a site slow or dated. It makes it unreachable for most visitors. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all show a full-page warning that the connection isn’t private, and most people leave instead of clicking through. If the site uses HSTS, a setting that tells browsers to connect only over secure links, there is often no way to click through at all, and visitors are blocked outright until the certificate is fixed.

The damage doesn’t stop at the home page. Checkouts, contact forms, and logins that depend on the secure connection fail along with it, often without an error message that points at the real cause. Other systems break, too, because apps and integrations that call your site over a secure link refuse to connect to an expired certificate.

Nothing about your site has to change for any of this to happen. A date passes, and a site that worked on Friday is down on Monday. In a 47-day lifetime, that date comes around about every six weeks.

Automatic renewal tools do the heavy lifting well. The failures happen around them:

Look at the five failures above and you’ll see what they share. Each one happens quietly. The renewal job ran, or looked like it did, and nobody checked what the server was actually serving afterwards. Automation can tell you it tried. It can’t tell you the result reached your visitors.

What closes that gap is a check that never relies on your server’s own account of events. Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring does exactly that. It reads the certificate installed on your web server from the cloud, the way a visitor’s browser would, and alerts you before it expires, using thresholds you choose. If a renewal fails quietly, you hear about it from the monitor and not from a customer.

For each certificate, it records the issuing authority, the owner, the issue date, the expiration date, and the days remaining, including on servers that host several certificates behind one address. That last number matters more as lifespans shrink. When a certificate lasts 47 days, the days left is the figure that tells you a renewal is overdue, and you can set your warning against it using the quarter-of-the-lifetime rule covered next.

Once a monitor is watching your certificates, the next question is when it should speak up.

Most expiration alerts are set to a fixed number of days: warn at 30 days left and escalate at seven. That works for a certificate that lasts a year and renews with a month to spare. It breaks when the whole certificate lasts for a limited number of days.

Here’s why: a healthy certificate renews with about a third of its life still left. If your alert appears earlier than that, it goes off on certificates that are doing nothing wrong, and soon everyone ignores it. As lifespans shrink, a fixed 30-day alert will start doing exactly that.

The fix is to set the alerts based on lateness, not on how close the expiry date is. Warn when a quarter of the lifetime is left, since a renewal is overdue by then, and escalate when a tenth is left. Because these are shares of the lifetime, they keep working, however short lifespans get.

The next cut lands on March 15, 2027, so a few checks now will save you from scrambling later:

Shorter lifespans won’t break your site, but a missed renewal will, so fix the quiet failures now while a mistake still costs an afternoon to fix, not a Monday morning outage affecting lots of customers.

If you’d like a second pair of eyes on your certificates, you can start a 30-day free trial of Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring.

The DRAM and NAND shortages have driven SSD prices through the roof, but we've still managed to track down some of the best Black Friday SSD deals around. There are several 1TB and 2TB NVMe SSDs on sale — by far the most popular capacities — for less than $0.15 per GB from brands like MSI, Adata, Biwin, and Kingston. Normally, we're using price per GB as our north star here to make sure you're getting the best value for the drive you pick up.

All of the drives we've rounded up here are PCIe 4.0 SSDs, and they range in performance. Short of one exception for the 1TB and 2TB capacities, these are DRAM-less SSDs. Naturally, SSDs with a DRAM cache are more expensive. There are good deals on high-end drives like the Samsung 9100 Pro 2TB at 49% off, but we're focused on value options here. If you need more capacity, the T-Force G50 Evo 4TB at $399 is the best deal we've found.

A couple of the drives here are cheaper than when we reviewed them, in some cases a few years ago before the SSD pricing crisis took hold. Things are starting to turn in a positive direction with some of these discounts, though we still have a long way to go before we reach early 2025 pricing.

The Biwin Black Opal NV7400 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD with maximum read speeds of up to 7,450 MB/s, and maximum write speeds of up to 6,500 MB/s.

The Biwin Black Opal NV7400 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD with maximum read speeds of up to 7,450 MB/s, and maximum write speeds of up to 6,500 MB/s.

If you're looking for the cheapest 1TB NVMe SSD on Black Friday, the Kingston NV3 has the NV7400 beat out by $8. It too is a DRAM-less drive, and it comes with lower-rated specs than the NV7400 at 5,000 MB/s and 3,000 MB/s sequential reads and writes, and an endurance rating of 320 TBW for the 1TB capacity.

The Kingston NV3 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD that sports sequential read speeds of up to 6,000 MB/s and sequential write speeds of up to 4,000 MB/s.

Kingston's budget drives like the NV3 use somewhat of a grab bag approach to components, swapping out the controller and flash for whatever's available at the time. The 2TB is actually $30 less than the list price when we reviewed it more than four years ago; check out our full MSI Spatium M470 review. Granted, PCIe 4.0 drives were more expensive four years ago than they were two years ago, but it's still a positive pricing move given how expensive SSDs have become.

The Adata Legend 860 is a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD with 6,000 MB/s and 5,000 MB/s sequential read/write performance and a three-year warranty.

#10234. Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Picture this. A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later. Congratulations, you now have a customer's name, phone number and card details sitting in a plain text log file that half the engineering team can open.

This happens more often than people admit. Logging AI calls is genuinely useful, but prompts and responses are some of the most personal text your application ever touches. Here's how to keep the usefulness and drop the risk.

A regular web request is easy to log: URL, status code, time taken. AI calls are messier.

The output changes from run to run. If a user says "your bot gave me a wrong answer yesterday", the only proof of what happened is what you sent and what came back at that moment. You can't just replay it and expect the same result.

Prompts are also built, not typed. The final text is usually a template, a few retrieved document chunks, some chat history and the user's message stitched together. When something looks off, the bug could be in any of those pieces, and only the assembled prompt shows you which one.

Then there's cost. You pay by the token, so without per-call records you can't say which feature is burning money. And quality drifts over time as models get upgraded and templates get edited. Old logs are your only baseline.

So yes, you need these logs. The real question is what goes into them.

Before writing any masking code, agree on what counts as sensitive. In most business apps that means:

Names, emails, phone numbers and home addresses

Card numbers, bank details and government ID numbers

Health, legal or job-related details people mention in free text

Internal material like contract wording, pricing rules or source code

The first three groups follow patterns, so they're easy to catch. The last two don't, and that's where most teams get caught out. Keep that in mind, because it shapes the design below.

The safest sensitive value is the one that never reaches the log. So split what you record into two buckets.

The first is metadata: a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. None of this is personal, and it answers most day-to-day questions.

The second is content, meaning the actual prompt and response text. You only need this when you're investigating quality, and even then you rarely need all of it. A sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call.

Here's a mistake that's easy to make: letting the log appender clean things up afterwards. By then the raw text may already be in a buffer, an async queue or a crash dump. Mask first, then log.

The cleanest way is one small component that every AI log call has to pass through:

public interface PiiMasker {     String mask(String input); }

Nothing else is allowed to write raw prompts. One chokepoint is much easier to review and test than masking sprinkled across fifty classes.

For structured data like emails, cards and tokens, regular expressions do the job well:

public class RegexPiiMasker implements PiiMasker {     private static final Map RULES = new LinkedHashMap<>();     static {         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9.%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"), "[EMAIL]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?\d{10}\b"), "[PHONE]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("(?i)bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9.~+/=-]+"), "Bearer [TOKEN]");     }     @Override     public String mask(String input) {         if (input == null || input.isBlank()) return input;         String result = input;         for (var rule : RULES.entrySet()) {             result = rule.getKey().matcher(result).replaceAll(rule.getValue());         }         return result;     } }

A few small choices matter here. The patterns are compiled once, not on every call. The order is fixed, because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. And the replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable, so whoever debugs it later can still follow what the user was asking.

Regex won't catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence. For those you have a few options, and they work best together.

You can run a named-entity recognition model that tags people, places and organisations, then mask anything above a confidence threshold. You can do exact replacement of values you already know, such as the customer's name from the current session. Or, best of all, you can mask at the field level while building the prompt. If your code knows that customer.getEmail() is going into the template, swap in a placeholder right there instead of trying to spot it afterwards. Knowing beats guessing every time.

Plain redaction can remove too much. If the same email shows up five times in a conversation, five identical [EMAIL] tags hide the fact that it was one person.

The fix is consistent pseudonyms. Turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. You can still follow the thread, but nobody can read the original from the log. Use an HMAC with a secret from your secrets manager. A plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes, because there just aren't that many phone numbers.

One warning: if you also store a lookup table to reverse the tokens, that table is now sensitive data too. Most teams are better off with one-way tokens.

Free-text log lines are hard to search and easy to leak through. Write one JSON record per AI call with clearly separate fields:

log.info("ai_call",     kv("requestId", requestId),     kv("model", model),     kv("promptVersion", "support-reply-v4"),     kv("inputTokens", usage.inputTokens()),     kv("outputTokens", usage.outputTokens()),     kv("latencyMs", elapsed),     kv("promptMasked", masker.mask(prompt)),     kv("responseMasked", masker.mask(response)));

Now dashboards for cost and latency never need to touch the text fields at all. You can also keep the two kinds of data for different lengths of time: metadata for a year, masked content for a couple of weeks. Put the request ID into your logging framework's MDC so every line belonging to one call, including retries and tool calls, carries the same ID.

Streaming trips people up. Tokens arrive in tiny pieces, and a card number can be split across two chunks, which means masking each chunk on its own will miss it. Collect the full response in a buffer, mask it once the stream ends, and log that. If the stream dies halfway, run the partial buffer through the same masker.

Tool calls are the other trap. When the model calls one of your Java methods, the arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the whole exchange: order details, account balances, addresses. Treat them as part of the prompt and response. Log the tool name, duration and outcome by default, and log arguments only after masking.

Masking lowers the risk but never removes it, so surround it with some ordinary discipline:

Give content fields a short retention period. Old prompt archives are liabilities.

Limit who can read AI logs. Debugging a model doesn't mean someone needs to read customer messages.

Encrypt log storage and the pipeline that feeds it.

Log the hashed user ID so you can find and delete one person's records when they ask.

Allow verbose logging in development with fake data, and enforce strict settings in production through configuration, not through people remembering.

A masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none, because everyone assumes the logs are clean. Write tests for it:

@Test void masksEmailAndCardNumber() {     String raw = "Contact me at asha@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111";     String safe = new RegexPiiMasker().mask(raw);     assertFalse(safe.contains("asha@example.com"));     assertFalse(safe.contains("4111"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[EMAIL]"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[CARD]")); }

Build a small set of messy, realistic samples: numbers with odd spacing, mixed languages, addresses inside sentences, text pasted from spreadsheets. Run them in your CI pipeline, and add a new case every time a leak turns up. A scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net too.

A few I'd watch for. Logging raw text at debug level and assuming production never enables it; debug flags get switched on during incidents, so mask at every level. Masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results. Letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs. Leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, which bypasses your masker completely. And treating masking as finished once it ships, when every new prompt template can bring new kinds of data.

Every AI call writes a structured metadata record with a request ID

All prompt and response text goes through a single masker first

Streams are masked after assembly, and tool arguments are masked too

Content logging is sampled, short-lived and access-controlled

Tests cover the masker, with a regression case for every past leak

Client libraries aren't dumping raw payloads into the logs

Good logs turn an AI feature from a black box into something you can actually debug, price and improve. The same logs can also expose the people who trusted you with their details. The way through is fairly plain: record metadata for every call, push all content through one well-tested masker, use pseudonyms when you need to follow a conversation, handle streams and tools carefully, and keep retention short. Set that up before launch, not after the first incident, and you get visibility without regret.

We update this index regularly with the lowest prices available in the U.S. market for each memory kit. Our tracker covers a range of capacities and speeds across both budget and premium brands. Retailers are taking advantage of the DRAM shortage, just as they did with the graphics card shortage a few years ago. They've started raising DDR5 prices to align with current market conditions and sometimes bundle DDR5 memory kits with processor or motherboard purchases.

Say hello to a new 3D printer and goodbye to wasteful filament “poop.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tool changers — 3D printers with multiple heads — have been a major focus of the industry for more than a year, and for good reason. Multiple heads mean you don’t have to purge the nozzle every time your print swaps colors or materials, which has the dual benefit of making complex prints much faster while saving a massive amount of filament waste or “poop,” which is a problem with more traditional multi-color AMS, single-toolhead printers.

But while these tool changers typically cost multiple thousands of dollars a few years ago, they’ve gotten much more affordable in the past year, starting with Snapmaker’s sub-$1,000 U1 (now just $699) and then Fashforge’s Creator 5 not long after. And both of those printers, plus a traditional four-color AMS printer designed to minimize wasted filament, are all on sale at their lowest-ever prices as we head into Black Friday.So if you’re thinking of diving into the 3D printing realm or your existing printer is getting long in the tooth, now is a great time to make the leap to a tool changer and see how it can change your printing game — or perhaps your printing business.

Snapmaker’s U1 kicked off the affordable tool changer craze around this time last year, with an early Kickstarter price of $799 and a full retail price of $999. But now it’s widely available and on sale for $100 less than ever. When we reviewed the U1, we praised its roomy build area (270 mm cubed), direct-drive tool heads, and its four-head tool-changing capabilities, earning it 4.5 stars and a spot on our best 3D printers list.

Last year, this tool-changer was the most anticipated upcoming printer around. With four heads for swapping colors or materials without the need to "poop," it can breeze through complex multicolor prints much faster than single-head printers, without wasting nearly as much filament.

On the heels of the U1, Flashforge released the Creator 5, a tool changer that’s a bit more basic, but still a solid machine (we gave it 4 stars in our review), priced even lower than the Snapmaker, both when it launched (at $699) and now, when it’s on sale for $100 less. You can grab that base model, or the Creator 5 Pro, which adds an enclosure with a cooling fan and filtration for more consistent temperatures, which can prevent warping and generally lead to better prints.

This open CoreXY 3D printer has four toolheads, is rated for head swaps that take 7 seconds, and sports a 256 mm X3 build volume.

An upgraded version of the Creator 5, you get the same 4 tool heads and build volume, now with an enclosed chamber with a fan and filter. If you're sensitive to PLA or PETG fumes, your workspace lacks ventilation (or is drafty), or you print with more exotic filaments, it's worth paying extra for.

Last up, and least expensive on this list, is Anycubic’s Kobra X. This isn’t a tool changer, as it has a single head. Instead, it’s a more traditional four-color printer that aims to reduce filament waste by putting the filament cutter much closer to the nozzle tip. It also takes up less space, as it's designed to keep four filament spools on a rack up top rather than a separate AMD.I’ve owned this printer for going on a year, and you’ll still see a lot of filament waste when tackling multi-color prints, but it does create less poop than previous printers I’ve owned. And if you can’t afford to spend more than $500, the Kobra X delivers solid multi-color printing at a price that’s tough to beat. It’s currently on sale for its lowest-ever price of just $279.

This low-priced, space-saving four-color 3D printer has a 260 mm X3 build volume, houses four filament spools up top, and is quick when swapping filaments. It also saves filament waste by cutting closer to the nozzle tip when switching, but it will still "poop," and can waste a lot of filament if you regularly tackle multi-color prints.

#10230. GrapheneOS shows off how it plans RCS support without Google Messages

As virtually all Android phones and now iPhone support RCS messaging, the standard is key to communication in 2026. But GrapheneOS users, by default, are still stuck with SMS/MMS as RCS is typically locked behind Google Messages on Android.

It’s a problem that Graphene’s developers have been trying to work out for a while now, and it seems progress is being made. A proof-of-concept messaging app with RCS was shared on Twitter/X, showing Graphene’s RCS implementation working with both Google Messages and iOS with end-to-end encryption and full features including typing indicators and reactions.

While this app skips the need to use Google Messages directly, the app does still use Google’s services as most carriers rely on Google for RCS. GrapheneOS still needs a sandboxed version of Google Play, for now, for this to work, but the developers say that a standalone version for carriers that support Google-less RCS will be coming.

We made a proof of concept RCS messaging app. It already has end-to-end encryption with MLS compatible with Google Messages and iOS, typing indicators, delivery/read receipts, reactions and media/file sharing. We'll use what was learned to integrate RCS into our Messaging app. pic.twitter.com/jzCTCCKrIQ

There’s still no firm timeline for this new RCS support on GrapheneOS, but Google Messages can still be used in the meantime.

The final update today will make AI Overviews and AI Mode responses “more personally relevant.”

So if you’ve been researching and planning for a trip, you can pick up right where you left off in a new search thread without starting over or repeating yourself. As always, you can adjust or turn off personalization at any time in your Search Settings.
